speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. Sir SAM HUGHES (Victoria) presented the first report of the special committee appointed to act with a like committee of the Senate in determining the form of a memorial to be erected in the Parliament Buildings to the late Colonel Baker, as follows:
The Special Committee appointed to confer and act with a like Committee of the Senate in determining the form of the memorial to be erected in the Parliament Buildings to the late Lieut-Colonel Baker, MP., beg leave to present the following as their first report:
At the request of the committees, made during the last session of Parliament, Major R. Tait MacKenzie, a noted Canadian artist and sculptor, prepared two alternative sketches of the proposed memorial, and at a recent meeting of the committees in joint session, the sketches were submitted and explained by Major Tait MacKenzie. Mr. John Pearson, architect of the Parliament Buildings, was present, and his views were also considered as to the merits of the suggested designs.
After several meetings and careful considera-ion, your committee beg to recommend that the site for the proposed memorial selected by your committee during the last session of Parliament and approved by both Houses be adhered to.
That the memorial be a figure in stone, about six feet six inches in height, in high relief, carved to a likeness of the late Lieut.-Colonel Baker in military uniform, and set in a shallow niche on a pedestal four feet in height; the figure itself and the background to l.c made out of a solid block of limestone, which would replace the part of the wall in the site chosen by your committee last session.
It is submitted that a figure in stone, in preference to a bronze figure, would fit in more harmoniously with the architecture of the building, and forming part of the building, would be a more fitting tribute to one who so gallantly laid down his life for the Empire.
With regard to the inscription on the proposed memorial, your committee recommend that the following be inscribed on the front of the pedestal:
"Lieutenant-Colonel George Harold Baker, M.P., Fifth Canadian Mounted Rifles,
Killed in action, June second, 1916,
At the battle of ' Sanctuary Wood.' Erected by order of the Parliament of Canada." and that the selection of suitable inscriptions for the right and left sides of the figure be submitted in a subsequent report of your committee, and for this purpose your committee further recommend that they be given leave to sit again, and to report from time to time.
A clay model in miniature of the memorial is on view in room No. 534.
Your committee have been informed by Major MacKenzie and the architect that the estimated cost of the proposed memorial will be in the neighbourhood of $12,000, and your commute i* teg to recommend that such an amount be placed in the Supplementary Estimates at the present session to defray the cost of the said memorial.
All of which is respectfully submitted.

Rt, Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister) moved:
That on and after Saturday, the 29th instant, until the end of the present session the House shall sit on Saturdays, and that the order of business on Saturday shall be the same as on Friday; and also, that on and after Tuesday, the 1st June next, until the end of the present session, the House shall meet at 11 o'clock in the morning of each day except Sundays, and in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall also be an intermission every day from one to three o'clock, p.m.
Be said:	We have now entered upon
the fourth month of the session, and there is a good deal of business still on the Order Paper. Representations have been made to me from both sides of the House that we should sit longer hours and should sit on Saturdays. I hope that the House will be willing to accept the motion for these reasons. I have not yet had an opportunity of making to my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King) the statement with regard to further business which I promised a day or two ago, but I am entirely in the hope that it will not be necessary for the Government to bring down any further measures of a controversial character.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am
sure that every hon. member of the House appreciates the Prime Minister's motive m desiring to have the proceedings of this session brought to a conclusion as speedily as possible to permit hon. members to return to their homes and give some attention to their private business. I feel it a public duty however, to point out that, with the Government's programme what it is, and the progress we have thus far made being what it is, it would appear to be very much against the public interest that we on this side should, at this stage of the proceedings of the House, acquiesce in the resolution which my right hon. friend has moved.
We are here for the purpose of giving attention to the public business of Canada. A certain amount of 'the country's business

has been brought before us; but we have on the Order Paper notice of other legislation that is to be introduced, of which we have no particulars at the present time, and we have still before us for completion the main work of the session. May I point out that it is no fault of hon. gentlemen on this ' side, nor, indeed is it the fault of any hon. member of the House that we have reached this season of the year with so little accomplished in the transaction of the principal business of this session. If little has been accomplished thus far, it is certainly the fault of the Government, first of all in having called the session so late in the year, and secondly, in being so tardv in bringing down much of their important legislation.
May I point out what seems to me to be the effect of the motion of my right hon. friend? Only nine days ago, on May 18, the Budget was introduced, and it is recognized throughout the Dominion that it is one of the most important Budgets this Parliament, has ever been called upon to consider. It is suggested that we shall sit morning, afternoon and night, six days in the week, Saturday being included. In addition to the Budget, we have still before us the Franchise Bill, which is -another of the most important pieces of legislation ever -introduced into this House. We have considered in committee a large part of the Franchise Bill, but the most contentious clauses still remain. Then there are the Estimates of the different departments of the Government, and thus far Parliament has had opportunity to consider little or nothing with respect to past public expenditures or appropriations for the ensuing year. I have made a summary of what has been passed thus far in the way of Estimates. On March 23, some Estimates in respect to shipbuilding were passed; on March 30, an item of the Estimates of the Railway Department; on April 15, the Civil Service bonus, (one-sixth of the amount); on April 23 and May 6, Estimates of the Department of Marine and Fisheries; on April 26, Soldiers' Land Settlement Estimates. That is practically all that this House has thus far considered of the Estimates. Yet, this Parliament is to be asked to expend for the public service in the ensuing year an amount running into many millions of dollars.
The Government's motion means this: that we are called on to deal with the most important matters before the country under conditions where each member will be obliged to give morning, -afternoon and

night to the proceedings of the House. In other words, it looks as though the Government had sought to bring about what 1 would call "one big drive," whereby to jam through the House legislation of vital importance to the country under conditions which make impossible proper attention, consideration, or criticism. It is physically impossible for members to si't here morning, afternoon and night, six days in the week, and give to legislation of this importance the attention it ought to receive.
Let me direct the attention of the House to the Bills that you, Mr. Speaker, have called within the last few minutes. On the Order Paper, under the heading "Introduction of Bills," there is the following list of Bills still to be introduced by the Government :
An Act to amend The Insurance Act, 1917.
An Act to amend the Criminal Code.
An Act to amend the Penitentiary Act.
An Act to amend the Trade Mark and Design Act.
An Act to amend the Irrigation Act.
An Act to amend the Admiralty Act.
An Act to amend The Naturalization Act, 1919.
An Act to amend the Juvenile Delinquents Act.
An Act to amend the Prisons and Reformatories Act (Nova Scotia).
Either these are meaningless bite of legislation, or they are very important measures. If they are important measures, members of this House should have opportunity of studying them before they are called upon to register their votes for or against their several clauses. There will be no opportunity for any hen. member to get into communication with his constituents or other parties who are interested in the legislation; or to realize what public opinion as reflected in the press may be as regards these measures if they are pressed under such conditions.
We have yet to deal with practically all of the Estimates; we have the consideration of all the resolutions mentioned in the Budget ; we have the contentious clauses of the Franchise Bill. .My right hon. friend has just assured us that there will be nothing further of a controversial nature, which is a fortunate thing, but I shall be very much surprised if we do not have to consider further Supplementary Estimates or something other of a nature which should receive careful attention. In the public interest, therefore, it is desirable that at this stage we should ask ourselves just what is expected of members of Parliament who are sent here to transact the business of the country. I can well understand that every hon. member is feeling very keenly the sacrifice he is making in being absent from his home and not having an opportunity of attending to his private business-. I can realize, particularly in the case of many -members from the West where the seasonal nature of their callings requires their presence at this time of the year, that they would like to be ah home attending to their work, and not be obliged to have someone else look after it or else leave it undone. These may be reasons for the Government -considering what -may be owing hon. members in the matter of indemnities to which they may -be entitled under conditions as they now exist in the country, and as they have developed since the war. -But I contend that the first duty of a member of Parliament is to give his time to public work, and that he should not seek to hurry through important legislation so that he can get back to his private business. I hope the Prime Minister will appreciate the force of these few remarks, which I make simply because I believe it is all-important in the public interest that the business of the House should not he rushed through with undue haste.
May I point out this to my hon. friends opposite? As the Prime Minister has mentioned, we have been in session for three months and are now entering upon the fourth month. The time of this Parliament has been taken up for the -most part with amending legislation passed at previous sessions of this very Parliament, many of which amendments have been rendered necessary solely because of the undue haste with which this legislation had been rushed through at a previous session. I have a list of the legislation which has thus far been considered, and I will draw the attention of the Prime Minister to the extent to which the time of the House has been taken up, at the instance of the Government, with a lot of second rate measures- -because that is all they amount to-to the exclusion of the important work of the session. We have had before is, for example, .an Act respecting the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, to amend a section regarding pensions which -bad already -been amended in 1919. We have had the Franchise Bill, which is in reality a re-enactment of an old measure with additional amendments. There was an Act to amend the Currency Act, 1910, which Act had been amended at the first session of 1919 and has come in for further amendment at this session. There was an Act to

amend and consolidate the Acts relating to patents of invention. This Act was amended in the first session of 1919, and again in the second session of 1919. There was an Act to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act, another Act that had been passed previous to the session of 1919 and which was amended in 1919. This session still further amendments are brought in. Other measures are the following: An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, previously amended at several sessions, including the first and second sessions of 1919; an Act respecting Food and Drugs, a'so amended at both the first and second sessions of 1919; an Act respecting Commercial Feeding Stuffs, amended at the second session of 1919; an Act to amend the Dominion Lands Act, previously amended at the first and second sessions of 1919. An Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, previously amended at. the first and second sessions of 1919; an Act to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918, and the Civil Service Amendment Act, 1919; an Act to confirm the agreement between the Grand Trunk Railway and His Majesty, which the Government admitted was presented to Parliament to correct certain errors that had been made, and made on account of the undue haste with which the measure had been rushed through at the last session of Parliament; an Act to amend tl e Technical Education Act, which had been amended at the first session of 1919, an Act to amend the Industrial Disputes Act, 1907, which had been previously amended in 1918 and was further amended ibis year, much, I think, to the disadvantage of the legislation; an Act to amend the Soldier Settlement Act, amended in 1919; an Act to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, previously amended in 1918; an Act to amend the Canada Shipping Act, previously amended in the first and second sessions, 1919; an Act to amend the Oleomargarine Act passed in 1919; and finally an Act to amend the Inspection and Sale Act, previous amendments to which were made in 1918.
There is a long legislative programme, bat what does it amount to? It is simply bringing back to this Parliament, to occupy the time of members of this House, a lot or legislation to be amended, some of the amendments being wholly secondary and unimportant. On the face of it, it is a confession that in previous years the Government's legislation was so ill-digested that within a year they have had to come 
back to Parliament for further amendments.
I fear that the way we shall be rushing tl,rough legislation in the next few weeks, if we have morning, afternoon, and evening sittings, will mean that the time of another session, a year hence, will be taken up again with a lot of further amendments of this sort.
1 might also direct the attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the fact that we have not yet obtained from the Government a statement of the Civil Service classification. We shall be called upon to vote appropriations for the Civil Service. In the Estimates presented to Parliament this year, the explanatory details of Civil Government usually printed are omitted. I hardly think the country will expect Parliament to pass the appropriation necessary for Civil Government until we get these essential details.
There are also several important reports that have not yet been brought down: There has been no report, as far as I can see, of the Public Printing and Stationery, the Militia Council, the Geological Survey, Mines Branch, the Penitentiaries Branch, Department of Justice, and the Archives Branch. Then we have no Parliamentary documents from the Department of Trade and Commerce relating to Steamship Subsidies, the Trade of Canada, Grain Commissioners, Criminal Statistics, Weights and Measures, Dominion Statistics.
We have not yet had the railway statistics brought down. It was only seven days ago that the Minister of Railways presented to this House the report of the Department of Railways and Canals, and it was only thirteen days ago that the fourth Volume of the Auditor-General's report was presented to the House. Yet hon. members of this House are supposed to have mastered the details of these different reports. The reports a!re supposed to have been presented to the people's representatives in this House, and we are supposed to have examined the legislation that is before Parliament in the light of these different documents. Mr. Speaker, it makes Parliamentary government a farce when legislation is proceeded with in that fashion. That is not the procedure that ought to be adopted or followed by a deliberative assembly. As I said, it may be a satisfactory method of conducting warfare. It may be one way of effecting a great drive so that there will be great confusion when millions of dollars of the people's money are about to be voted, but it is not the method which should be adopt-

ed in a deliberative assembly having the responsibility which this Parliament is called upon to exercise. I hope under the circumstances that my right hon. friend will consider, first, the public interest, and secondly, the private wishes of individual members.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret I was not in the Chamber when file Prime Minister made his statement regarding the resolution we are now discussing. I have listened with much interest to the speech of the leader of the Opposition-of the Opposition at that end of the Chamber. First, I would offer just one word of criticism of the Government in the most friendly way. I think they have been a little dilatory this session in brnging down the legislation which they had to present to Parliament. While absent through illness, I read the reports of the debates, and I feel that considerable time was lost in the first six or eight weeks of the session. Might I suggest that the Government in future get its legislation down before the House a little earlier in the session?
There is a good deal of force in the arguments advanced by the leader of the Opposition. We are here concerned with serious business. We have yet the greater part of the Estimates to consider and pass upon, and the expenditure of large sums of the public money at this time ought to be careful!;; scrutinized. Nevertheless, on the other hand, X feel that for the members' from Western Canada and the Maritime Provinces there is a real hardship in sitting here a greater length of time than is absolutely necessary. Being a man of peace, and this little group around me being men of peace also, may I offer a suggestion to the Prime Minister and the leader of the Opposition? It is this, that we defer Saturday sittings until perhaps a week or two weeks, from next Saturday, and that instead of having mornings sittings we assemble at two o'clock in the afternoon from the beginning of next week, and continue to meet at that hour until the end of the session. I believe that in that way we could accomplish as much work as by morning sittings. The position of hon. members in regard to morning sittings is this:	Some of the committees are still at work. All hon. members have correspondence to look after, they must study the legislation before the House, and have to attend to other matters that are coming up daily. With morning sittings we have no opportunity to attend to all this. With lunch at one o'clock, I
see no reason why we could not assemble at two, sit till six, reassemble at eight and adjourn at the usual hour. I think that in that way we should make just as much progress as by having morning sittings. Being a humble individual I offer this, suggestion to the Government and the leader of the Opposition for their consideration.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have on more than one occasion voiced my feelings and opinions in connection with the work of the House. Living three thousand miles away, I have come here for the purpose of transacting the public business, as we all have, as has been stated by the leader of the Opposition. It has been my desire to attend to that work regularly, and I believe that I am one of the members who attend the sittings of the House as assiduously as possible. My grievance is this:	that by arrangement
between the two whips in this House hon. gentlemen across the aisle leave here on Friday afternoon and return on Monday night, as do hon. members on this side of the House from the province of Ontario, and the quorum in this House from Friday until Monday is maintained by the members from the West, until these other gentlemen have attended to the pleasure of their families and their business at home.
As to the accusation of the leader of the Opposition, that this Government was attempting to make a drive in the last days of the session, I would remind him of the fact that last session he was very desirous of going home at an early stage of the game. So far as the measures on the Order Paper are concerned, they have been on the Order Paper for the last two months and it is the fault of hon. members themselves if they are not familiar with the proposed legislation. My hon. friend has touched upon indemnities. Let him rise in his seat now and say he is in favour of increased indemnities.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: Well, well.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
So faT as I am
concerned, I have no objection to remaining here twelve months if it is necessary, and I am paid for it, but under the present schedule of pay I am not willing to remain here while the members from Quebec and Ontario enjoy themselves at the opening of jockey club meets or at home, or attend to their office and business three days in the week while the members from the West are left here to transact the public business. Those gentlemen take temporary rooms in

Ottawa, but we are required to sign leases for six months if we desire to have permanent quarters. Our friends opposite go home on Friday and save money by leaving the city, and in addition to this they enjoy the great advantage of spending considerable time with their families. We, on the other hand, are compelled to remain here continuously. We on this side are anxious to carry on the business of the country without interruption, but we have not the advantage of saving money, as hon. gentlemen from Ontario and Quebec who are objecting to this have by taking temporary rooms and going home at regular intervals. I think that the suggestions of the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) come with bad grace. We all regret, I am sure, his absence from the House recently through illness, but we have had to attend constantly to the business of the House; and if the hon. gentleman had devoted less time to the organizing of the Farmers' party in the East he would have been in a position to know more of the business of this session. There are no committees sitting that will embarrass the attendance of hon. gentlemen in the House. Within the last week no committees, except one, have been considering any business of the House, and yet 1 may point out the fact that the attendance on this side has been limited to three or four gentlemen, including the Minister of Finance-

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
That is the only truth in the hon. gentleman's speech.
Mr. H. A. MACKIE (Edmonton)-while last night there were but barely twenty hon. members opposite. Is not the hypocrisy of this matter apparent? Hon. gentlemen are putting forward the plea that they are eager to attend to the -business of the House, while as a matter of fact, at one sitting, there are only three members on this side and twenty members opposite, the Farmers' party being represented by one. Those hon. gentlemen who make professions of anxiety to attend scrupulously to the business of the House, should see to it, through the medium of their Whip, that they are in their seats while legislation is being put through, instead of attending to their own business at home. I want to go on with the business of the House so that I may be able to go home and attend to my own within a reasonable time.	.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
This is the second occasion on which the

hon. member has made the sweeping statement that all hon. gentlemen in this House coming from Quebec and Ontario go home on Friday and are absent on Monday. This general allegation on the part of my hon. friend opposite I do not want to- go unchallenged. There are many hon. members from Quebec and Ontario who are present in this House on Fridays and on Mondays as well; and I desire to tell my hon. friend, further, that all, or practically all the members from Quebec on this side of the House remain in the House every day of the week, Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays as well as the days on which he says they are absent. For the last two weeks we have sat in this House until twelve o'clock at night and sometimes one o'clock in the morning, and as the hon. gentleman has just truly remarked there have been occasions when there were only three or four hon. members present on the other side of the House. Sir, it is those gentlemen who remain here all the time, from three o'clock in the afternoon until twelve at night, that are entitled to some consideration in this matter. They give their full attention to the legislation that is brought before the House and study it with all the care it demands. They have to be here all the time, and it is unfair to ask those few-if there are only a few who so conscientiously attend to their parliamentary duties-to come back here at eleven o'clock in the morning after having spent a strenuous and trying day in this House until a late hour at night.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: A. MACKIE (Edmonton): May 1 ask my hon. friend a question? Is it not a fact that you have attended to your own private practice during the session,-something I have not done myself?

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: No Sir; it is not a fact. Let me tell my hon. friend that I have been here all the time; and I think I may fairly claim, Mr. Speaker, that I have been diligent in my attendance. I have endeavoured to give to the consideration of the public questions that come before this House that zealous study and attention which all legislation should receive.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
I am here promptly at three o'clock in the afternoon and I remain, not for a few moments and then go away; I stay, practically speaking, all the time. I say again, Mr. Speaker, that it is eminently unfair to ask me or any other hon. gentleman to come here at eleven

o'clock in the morning after spending a hard day in the House. There is no one in this House who would be more pleased to see the session over than myself.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: Except me.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: It is all right for hon. gentlemen carelessly to say, " Let us go home;" but we have something else to do, Mr. Speaker. Our mandate demands something more than that we shall just come here and, when it suits our .fancy, go home again irrespectively of what we may have done in the way of business. We must give to the legislation-to the Estimates and to all the business that comes before us-that consideration which the people expect us to give to our public duties. Business well considered is business well done; business rushed is business ill done; and it ill becomes hon. gentlemen who are seldom seen in their seats in this House to cheer their 'ellow members when they make the irresponsible suggestion that we should close up everything and go home.

subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext: I depreciate very much the practice of washing dirty linen in public and I also think that on the whole the proposition of the Prime Minister (Sir itobert Borden), being in accordance, as it is, with precedent of many years' standing, is a very good one. Personally I think we had better adapt ourselves as best we can to the common sense of the situation and let common sense guide us. For my part, I support the Prime Minister in this matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. JACQUES BUREAU (Three Rivers and St. Maurice) :
subtopic: MORNING AND SATURDAY SITTINGS.
speechtext:
I think we have strayed somewhat from the question under consideration, and my hon. friend from East Edmonton (Mr. Maickie) in his desire to make an argument vented a little grievance Which evidently he thinks he has. If the hon. gentleman bad stated that when members from Quebec and Ontario went home on Fridays and stayed away from the House they hampered the progress of the business of the House, he would have made some point. But that is not his contention. He simply says that some members can go home and spend time with their families, while he has to remain in Ottawa. Now, Sir, as the hon. gentleman from Red Deer has said, this question is one of common sense, and the point to be settled is this: how much can human nature endure, and to what extent can men be taxed physically if they are to perform their duties thoroughly? If we are going to come here at eleven o'clock in the
morning and sit until one, and then come back at three and sat until six, returning at eight and sitting indefinitely to all hours of the night, and sometimes until one or two in the morning-for the Minister of Militia (Mr. Guthrie) in his zeal in putting through the Franchise Bill showed an unmistakable tendency to adopt late hours-then it will be utterly impossible for hon. gentlemen to give anything like serious consideration to the work that comes before them. There are still some very important matters to be dealt with, Sir. The leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) just now read the list of Bills which still appear on the Order Paper, and one of which is a Bill to amend the Insurance Act of 1917. The Minister of Finance, who is to promote that Bill, knows that it involves very important considerations; and from correspondence and despatches I have received in connection with the matter, I may state that every big industry, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, is interested in that	Bill, which	will	affect	theirrates	of	insurance and will also
affect their business to a large extent. Now, these people have a right to get their views put before Parliament, but we cannot help them. As my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition has said, practically no Estimates have been brought down. The Budget is still under discussion, and we are told that the Government will require more money. Well, Mr. Speaker, the people are entitled to know what has been done with the money that has been already voted. When we voted one-sixth, of the appropriations I registered my protest, because I thought the Estimates ought to have been brought down, and that, except as to salaries, it was unfair to ask any hon. member to commit himself to any appropriation without first having an opportunity to express his views thereon, for the discussion of these Estimates is the only way whereby we can get the information we require.
As my hon. leader has said', the latter part of the Auditor General's Report has been brought down only recently, and the report of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Reid) has been on the Table only within the last six or seven days and contains very few details. Then, too, questions have remained on the Order Paper unanswered, or badly answered, and we have been unable to get further answers. When the Government do not want to answer a question, they just say: "Make it a motion for a return," and that question never sees the light of day again.

Although I am mot as young as many hon. members, I have as much endurance as any of my hon. friends, and I say that I cannot rightly do my duty if I have to be here at eleven o'clock in the morning until midnight. We on this side of the House have to be in our places anyway, but conditions are different on the other side, and my hon. friend from East Edmonton (Mr. Mackie) let the cat out of the bag. If the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) is in the House his colleagues need not be in attendance; and the same remark applies if any other minister is in his seat; but we have got to be here, anyway. Another circumstance that makes conditions easier for them than for us is that they know in advance by reports prepared by departmental officials what business is to be taken up, so their brief is prepared before they come to the House, and all they have to do is to put their case forward, and their work is done; but our work only then begins. And how are we going to do our work satisfactorily if we have to begin at eleven o'clock In the morning and continue until probably two o'clock next morning? I say it is a physical impossibility.
I realize, Mr. Speaker, that we are all desirous of going home. I realize the hardship of my hon. friends from the West and I sympathize with them at being separated from their families for such a long time. But I dismiss the argument of the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Mackie). We have to pay for our rooms the same as gentlemen from the West. I pay for my room by the week whether I am here or not, for I am not going to carry my rags home under my arm every Friday nigfht.

speechtext:
Some members from Quebec go home on Friday and spend less money than other hon. members who remain here. I may tell my hon. friend that it is not a question whether he spends more money than I do, or vice versa; it is a question whether common sense justifies the proposition to sit mornings and Saturdays. If we are humanly able to stand that pressure and discharge our duties satisfactorily, no objection can be urged; but I feel that I cannot endure the strain nor get through my work satisfactorily under such conditions.
It is just as great a hardship to me as to other hon. members not to be able to get

back to my office, perhaps more so, because I have not the means that some others have to render me independent of my profession; but in spite of that I am ready to do my duty and to sit here until September, if necessary. And every hon. member ought to be ready to do the same. As my hon. friend said, we are just at the crucial sections of the Franchise Act where we are certain of a conflict of opinion. We are only human, and the strain of long hours is bound.to tell on us. During the war we watched anxiously the morale of our troops; and if our electors watch our morale during two weeks of hot weather while we are sitting from eleven o'clock in the morning until the early hours of the following morning, I think they will notice a decline in it, and that those sections of the Franchise Act will be put through without proper discussion, simply because hon. members will be unable to give proper attention to them by reason of being physically unfit owing to attempting what is physically impossible. Besides, hon. members will not be fit otherwise, because they will not have sufficient time between two o'clock in the morning and eleven o'clock next morning to study the questions that ai 3 to engage their attention at the next sitting.
I do not think sitting on Saturdays will advance business at all. The suggestion to open the day's business at two o'clock I think is reasonable, and I for one am willing to accept that proposal, or we might even commence work at a quarter to two, but certainly not at eleven o'clock in the morning. For that reason I shall oppose the motion made by the Prime Minister.
Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister) Mr. Speaker,-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
it has never been the practice in my experience of twenty-four years to press a motion of this kind when it is seriously opposed by the other side of the House. Therefore, I would not think of doing so now in view of what has been said by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition.
But my hon. friend made one or two observations which I think require a reply

from me. If he is under the illusion that this Parliament sitting from the first day df January until the thirty-first day of December would pass legislation in such perfect form that it would never require any amendment, I fear that my hon. friend will be sadly disillusioned. I venture this statement also; that if he will look over the legislation of the past, under whatever Government it may be, he will find that the major portion consists in amendments of Acts already passed; and for this very good reason,-that almost every conceivable subject under the sun has been dealt with at some time or other, and further legislation, necessitated by new developments and new conditions, is ordinarily made by amendment to legislation already existing. I do not think therefore that the list of amendments which m,y hon. friend has placed before the House has any real significance so far as this particular question is concerned.
It is, of course, highly desirable that we should get on with the business of the House. When hon. gentlemen on the other side speak of hardship and difficulty, I am ready to give every consideration to what they say, but I would like to point out to them that if there be any hardship in beginning the session at eleven o'clock in the morning and continuing until perhaps midnight, the hardship is as severe upon members of the Government as it is upon hon. members.

speechtext:
In reply to the
statement by the hon. member for East Edmonton (Mr. Mackie) that the ministers were absent from their seats both yesterday afternoon and evening, that is true, but they were not absent from this building. The mere putting through of the routine business day by day occupies very considerable time, and of course there are questions of policy regarding legislation to be brought down which demand conferences during a considerable portion of the
day among the members of the Government. My hon. friends the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding), the member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and the member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) will readily recognize the truth of what I say in that regard. However, that is perhaps enough of those matters.
Just one word as to the legislation that has been brought down. I am informed that the Franchise Bill was introduced on the 26th day ol March, and that up to the present time no less than seventeen sittings of the Committee of the Whole House have been fieveted to the mea.-ure. I would venture to think that such a degree of activity does not indicate any remissness on the part of the Government. I am also told by my colleagues, who were here when I unfortunately had to be absent, the Government legislation has been ready on every day on which Government business could proceed, and that there has been no delinquency on the part of the ministry in bringing forward such legislation for the consideration of the House.
If my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition recalls the history of legislation in this House-since I have been a member of Parliament at least-he will remark this: That measures of corresponding importance debated in the early part of the session necessarily receive very much more of discussion at all events than measures introduced in the latter part of the session. That is necessarily the case.	It always has
been the case; it always*will be the case; and I do not think that in the future that lies before my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition he will ever be able to modify very seriously that condition o.f affairs so long as parliamentary institutions continue as they are. It is in the very nature o.f things. I admit that if it were believed possible that a remedy could be found it should be 4 p.m. sought; but in my public experience I have never yet been able to devise any remedy for that condition. It unfortunately has proved in the case of all governments in the years that aie behind us, that legislation introduced at a later stage of the session has sometimes gone through without the same attentive consideration that would be accorded to it in the early part of the session.
I am content to let the motion stand for the present and to consider the proposal made by the hon. member for Marquette for which I think a good deal may be said. The only purpose the Government has in

mind is to get on with the business of the House as expeditiously as possible consistently with the public interest; and to impose no undue hardship upon any hon. member on either side. That is our purpose and our desire. I shall let the matter stand, and d'iscusis it further with my hon. 'friend the leader of the Opposition.

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, May 26, the debate on the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Hon. W. S. Fielding.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the few remarks
I intend to offer I shall he as brief as possible so as no-t fo delay the much desired 'prorogation df Parliament. Moreover, the debate on the Budget has well nigh been exhausted, and I do not suppose that I oan add very much to the very brilliant addresses wMch have already been delivered. The Budget Speech of the Minister of Finance has at least Mr. Speaker, one great merit:	It faith-

fully reflects the financial situation of Canada to-day. If my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) will permit me, I will compare his speech to a little piece of art which I saw in an old cathedral during my last visit to Europe. Visiting the cathedral of Rouen I noticed in the rear portion of the cathedral a little font-a real piece of art-[DOT] designed I am told by an old monk who worked at it for years and years. The especial feature about that little font is that when the passing traveller looks within it he will find reflected there the whole of the magnificent proportions of the cathedral, but unfortunately is seen upside down and reduced to a miniature. The Budget Speech, Mr. Speaker, recalls to [DOT]my mind that little font I saw in the *Gothic cathedral at Rouen. It reflects the Canada of to-day but the picture is all topsy-turvy and how mighty small it is aftei being under the direction of hon. gentlemen opposite
However, Mr. Speaker, the present Minister of Finance, as has been stated on several occasions during this debate, is not responsible for the awkward position in which he finds himself, and if on the present occasion I cannot give him my support I, at least, can offer him my sincere sympathy. We are told that there will be no revision of the tariff in spite of the many promises that have been made to Parliament from year to [DOT] year within, at least, the last five years. [DOT]But of course we must face a revision of taxation. I do not object to income tax; indeed, I have advocated it. Nor do I object to any tax or impost on the luxuries of life. But speaking on behalf of my constituents; on behalf of the man on the street, I do strenuously object to any tax on the necessities of life. One has not to be much versed on political economy to know that the basic wants of man are threefold : food, clothing and shelter. These necessities, in a cold country like Canada, should not be taxed. Any tax on the necessities of life are a handicap to the labourer, to the worker; they press more heavily on the poor man than they do on any other man in the community. They also handicap the producers and work in restraint of trade. I shall not quote at this moment the various opinions on this subject as expressed by the newspapers of Canada on *both sides of politics, but I only wish to quote the opinion of the man on the street. Upon reading the tariff resolutions of the Finance Minister, one of my electors, a respected citizen of the 177
county of Maisonneuve who has quite a large family and who has only small earnings to support it, wrote me the following:
Automobiles for passengers; former duty, 10 per cent plus war tax 7J per cent-17i per cent; -present duty, 15 per cent, plus one per cent excise on wholesalers only; in reality, a reduction on the greatest luxury of the age. The duties-
And I agree with my correspondent.
The duties on automobiles should be at least 25 per cent; that much was expected by the [DOT] importers. As regards clothing, boots and shoes, if the principle of taxing luxuries is to be adopted-and it seems to be generally accepted as necessary-let luxuries be taxed, not necessities. The minimum prices on all these commodities subject to taxation should be raised at least 50 per cent.
Take shoes. There are several large manufacturers of shoes in the constituency which I have the honour to represent.
It is impossible to-day to buy a shoe such as everybody in towns and cities is obliged to wear for less than $10 to $12. What are generally called Oxford walking shoes for ladies cost from $12 to $16. Is it not absurd to fix the minimum price subject to taxation at $9? Take confectionery. Not long ago Laura Secord chocolates were selling at 70 cents a pound; they now ask SO cents, making an additional profit of five per cent for the company. They do not give or issue any slip or check to the customer ; how much of this will go to the Government? The cost of sugar at retail is 22 cents a pound. Is not tlia price of Page and Shaw's or Neilson's candies at $1.25 a pound high enough to warrant the imposition of the tax of ten per cent on the manufacturer and not on the common people, not on the consumer?
Take sporting goods. I have many young sturdy Canadians in my division of Maisonneuve. French-Canadian families as you are aware are large and the boys are all more or less sportsmen.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext: Baseball champions.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Yes, we have carried the honours on man>
occasions in Maisonneuve. Well, there is a tax of 50 cents and upwards on sporting goods. My correspondent says:
If there is one thing in which the young people of our towns and cities should be encouraged, it is the practice of sports for the maintenance of virility and health. The class in the community that is suffering most from the high cost of living is the salaried class, the wage-earning class, and this provision hits them almost exclusively. It is a provision that should be struck out.
Now, I have this remark to make regarding gold ornaments. Why should the Government not expropriate for coinage purposes all the gold mined, with the exception, for our provinces at least, of a certain quantity required for wedding rings and dental purposes? The



use of gold should be absolutely prohibited except where no substitute can be found, until our coinage reserve again reaches the fine percentage which it had attained in 1914.
Mr. Speaker, I have the greatest confidence in Mr. Breadner's ability. But Mr. Breadner, able as he is, faithful watch-dog of the treasury that he is. is not ubiquitous. I tell my hon. friend th^ Minister of Finance that the administration of his new law will be nothing less than a premium on fraud.
My hon. friend did not, in his Budget Speech, dilate on the question of expenditure. He is new in the saddle as Finance Minister; he should read the speeches delivered many years ago by that grand old man of England, William Ewart Gladstone, on the question of economy. Mr. Gladstone was, perhaps, never more eloquent than when he delivered his Budget speeches as Chancellor of the Exchequer, and he was not ashamed to proclaim the following truths:
A Chancellor of the Exchequer must he prepared to be unpopular ; he must learn how to say no to many requests which are made to him ; he must be cheeseparing.
If there ever was an occasion when the Minister of Finance should practise cheeseparing, that occasion is now. My hon. friend says-and I believe he is sincere- that he will check the expenditure, and he appeals to hon. members on both sides to do the same. With the combination around him, I am afraid that on that question, at all events, my hon. friend, to repeat a phrase well known in Canadian politics, will be "nothing but a fly on the wheel." Let me offer him another suggestion. I already made one the other day to the House; I said, for instance, that our rules should *be so amended that ministers of the Crown should have a right to appear before both Houses of Parliament, whether they belonged to the one or to the other. I say to-day that you shall not check the tremendous expenditures of this country, unless at the beginning of the session a special committee is appointed to supervise the Estimates which are to be submitted to the House of Commons. That committee should have a right to send for books, to call for witnesses and experts in order to bring before the House only such items of expenditure as should be considered by Parliament. This seems to me a practical question, and though the reform may appear to be somewhat Tadieal, circumstances justify its adoption.
Let my hon. friend pause and ponder after having read the startling figures which

were given to this House the other day by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). In 1914, the expenditure per head was, in round figures, $24; in 1920, it has re-ached the enormous sum of $75 per head of the population. In 1914, the gross debt per head of the population was $71.75; in 1920, it is $334.90. In 1914, the net debt- per head of the population was $43.49; in 1920, it -is $215. These are stupendous figures, and my hon. friend should commence at once to eliminate from the Estimates any expenditures which might well be postponed until after Canada has resumed the proud position she occupied when she was financially led by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's.
My hon. friend will, I hope, think I am sincere in my advocacy of a. reduction in military expenditure. The war is now over, and the Englishman, being a plausible man, having the sagacity we know he has, has disbanded all his troops, and he ie now hard at- work to recuperate the trade and commerce of old England. Let Canada do likewise. We should reduce to its minimum the military expenditure of this country.
There are vague rumours regarding a naval expenditure. Many years ago when the treasury was overflowing with surpluses, I strongly supported the expenditure of several millions for the creation of a Canadian navy, manned by Canadian officers and Canadian sailors and flying with the British ensign, the Canadian flag. But those days have gone by, and we are face to face with heavy commitments and huge deficits which will paralyse the financial possibilities of this country for many years to come. We have had a visit from Lord Jellicoe, and since that visit we have been favoured with only a vague general answer as to the intentions of the Government in regard to the proposed navy. I do not know the intention of the Government nor of the minister who is at the head of the Naval Department, but al-1 I can say, in all sincerity, is this: This is a time for Canada to build, not warships, but friendships. How will yo-u build friendships? By giving something to do to my good and genial friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). He requires some work in that department which was described many years ago, I think, by himself, as the fifth wheel of the Government coach. How will you build friendships? By letting the Minister of Trade and Commerce, instead of appointing semi-am-

bassadors to play at diplomacy at Washington and elsewhere, appoint [DOT]alert trade commissioners who will capture wider markets for Canada and will meet the competition, not only of Americans, but of Australians, New Zealanders, yes, and Britons too.
On this subject, we might learn a lesson from old England, from her political economy and her commercial sagacity. I was amused the other day, listening to my good friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) lecturing old England. Poor old England, in the throes of bankruptcy! Poor old England, having been the dupe of free trade for half a century! In fact, imy hon. friend said: "But new days have come, new times have arisen in England and Mr. Asquith himself-and he coupled with the name of Mr. Asquith that o'f Mr. Lloyd George-appointed a commission four years ago to study the question of key industries. I asked my hon. friend if recommendations had been made. My hon. friend answered in the affirmative, but he failed to tell me if the Parliament of Great Britain had put into concrete form on the Statute Book any of the recommendations o'f that commission. I thought my hon. friend knew more about England than I did. I have been only a few times in the Old Country, but I know this: John Bull is a practical and shrewed business man. There are, it is said, two great safety valves in England. There is a safety valve to protect England against the agitator, and you might see that safety valve at work every Sunday morning in Hyde Park, where you hear the long-haired agitator disclaiming against Boyalty, against the House of Lords and generally against the institutions of the land.
