speechtext:
In 1919,
Mr. Speaker, a definite, well-planned and carefully worked out scheme was put into operation in the city of Winnipeg to destroy civil government in that city and in the province of Manitoba as a preliminary to destroying civil government all over this country. During that period Mistress Rose Henderson directed to the leader of the movement in the city of Winnipeg a letter - couched in these terms:
I am enclosing herewith a copy of the constitution of Soviets approved by I.enine and Trotsky. You can trust me implicitly, because you know that I was an advanced Socialist before I became a Bolshevist.
That was the ideal that Mrs. Rose Henderson held out before the people of the district of Timiskaming, and it was the organization known in this country as the One Big Union, whose principles she espouses, which supported the candidature of the hon. member for Timiskaming. I know that he is not a member of the One Big Union, and I say here again, with, I think, a full appreciation of my responsibility as a member of this House, that I do not believe the hon. member for Timiskaming himself appreciated the kind of campaign that was carried on to return him to this House. That is my opinion with regard to the hon. member. But I say that the One Big Union was the organization behind the campaign that elected him to this House, and that the ideals of that Union were preached in every mining camp in that constituency. And let me repeat, now that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) is in his seat, that when the time comes that hon. members professing the ideals of the hon. member for Marquette and his associates find it necessary to make use of the One Big Union in order to propagate their campaign of class hatred in this country, they have reached a fairly desperate condition.
In order that the House may know something about the ideals of the One Big Union-because I believe it is my duty to put this information before the House and the country-let me read the declaration of the chief organizer of the One Big Union, Mr. Fred G. Biedenkapp. I want the House to note the name B-i-e-d-e-n-k-a-p-p. The statement I am about to read is taken from the Chicago Times and is as follows:
Fred G. Biedenkapp, General Organizer ol the One Big Union, says the true communist and labour leader rejoices more over one unsuccessful strike than over ten strikes that succeed. What the O.B.U., and smaller organizations aim to create is not asking better working conditions for the average man but worse conditions. The workingman, or organization of workingmen, who strikes for higher wages and gets them, or for better working conditions and fewer hours of labour, and gets them, is not the material from which revolutionists are made. He is likely to be contented and take a conservative so-called sane view of a world in which the conditions have been easier and better for him. On the other hand, the striker, or group of strikers, who fails, are likely to be more embittered against the employers, the whole employing class and society generally and after repeated failures of this kind they will come to the conclusion that striking and voting are alike useless to improve the workingmen's lot, and they will listen to the Red who talks intelligently of direct action and the overthrow of society and

forms of Government as at present constituted. We have already two million workers, members of the O.B.U., and our numbers continue to grow as one unsuccessful strike follows another. Therefore, we, of the new vision, encourage strikes not because we desire to better the workingman's conditions but in order that they may fail-
Let me say right here, Mr. Speaker, that every regularly constituted body of organized labour in this country knows that the aim of the One Big Union is not to better the conditions of the workingmen; its aim is to destroy organized labour. Why? Because the men directing the One Big Union know that they cannot destroy organized society and organized forms of government as we now have them so long as legitimate organized labour continues to exist. I will go one step further, because I want to make my position absolutely clear. I assert that the One Big Union, whose principles I have just read, was the organization behind the election of the hon. member for Timis-kaming, who sits behind the hon. member for Marquette, and who is one of the latter's loyal supporters in this House.
The headquarters of the Independent Labour party in the town of Cobalt are in the One Big Union hall, because the organization of the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers has absolutely ceased to exist as an organized entity in the town of Cobalt, or in any other mining town in Northern Ontario, except one small branch in South Porcupine. As I say, the headquarters of the Independent Labour party, associated with the United Farmers of Ontario, are in the One Big Union hall. At the present time a suit is pending in the Ontario courts for possession of that particular property. The parties to that suit are, on the one hand, H. J. Everett, an officer of the Independent Labour party, and, on the other hand, an executive officer of the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers, Patrick James Redmond, and Charles H. Moyer, the president of the union. Why is that suit pending? Because an effort has been made to take the physical property of the International Union of Mine, Mill and Smelter Workers and to transfer it to the One Big Union organization, brought into this country to destroy legitimate organized labour. And let me repeat, that when hon. members find it necessary in their efforts to create class prejudice in this country to use an organization such as the One Big Union, in my opinion they have gone to pretty desperate lengths.
A few nights ago the hon. member for Red Deer said that 60,000 sons of Canada were
Mr. [Nicholson.!
sleeping in France and Flanders, and that they had died to release Canada from economic bondage. I know perfectly well that
60,000	of our sons are sleeping in France and Flanders, and that undoubtedly they died to save Canada.
But if my hon. friend from Red Deer were in the House to-night I would like to ask him this Question:	Does he think that
when his gallant boy stood beside my boy in the trenches in France and Flanders holding back the German line in those awful hours in 1918 when his heart strings and my heart strings were strained to the breaking point in the anxiety that the German forces would break through to the channel ports or take Paris, does he think that those boys had before their eyes the ideals of class prejudice and suspicion that he and his colleagues are preaching up and down the length of this country to-day? Mr. Speaker, if all the sacrifices of that awfhl war is for no other purpose than to bring about the condition suggested then I say that it is in the Providence of God, that those boys were taken to their rest before they were forced to live to see the awful futility of all that sacrifice. I say this further, Mr. Speaker, hon. gentlemen may say what they will, they may preach their doctrine as long as they wish, but here is one man that will fight tire hydraheaded monster of class prejudice and Bolshevism as long as the breath remains in his body.

subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I begin the few remarks I wish to utter to-night I think it would be appropriate for a moment or two to join issue with my hon. friend (Mr. Nicholson, Algoma), who has just resumed his seat with respect to certain assertions which he made. The hon. gentleman has informed us that he sees in the near future a lowering of the tariff to a greater extent than has taken place previously in the last forty years. Well, Mr. Speaker, like St. Thomas of old, I will wait and see before I accept the hon. gentleman's prediction in that regard.
The hon. gentleman has stated that the Grain Growers' Association is an organization that has been formed for the purpose of protecting its own interests. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that other associations are taking just as active a part in public affairs as the one to which he has alluded, the efforts of which may help to counterbalance whatever effects the hon. gentleman fears the Grain Growers Association mav produce. I refer particularly to an association to which reference was made

in the Montreal Gazette of 13th May last, as follows:
Million Dollar Fund for C.M.A.
Time to slam back at interests unfriendly to manufacturers.
So it would seem that the Canadian Manufacturers' Association is trying at the present time to raise a fund in order to protect its own interests against those of the rest of the community. Further, if we look at the end of the report to which the headings I have quoted relate we will see who are the members of the Manufacturers' Association. We shall see in that list some gentlemen who are the greatest supporters of the present Government and their policy. We see, for instance, Colonel Grant Mor-den, Sir James McKechnie, J. W. Norcross, W. F. Foster, B. W. Coughlin, Lieutenant-Colonel Sadler, and E. Bristol, M.P. In view of thgse facts I would ask my hon. friend whether the Government are likely t<f reduce the tariff to a greater extent than has been witnessed in the past when the association referred to is prepared to spend an enormous sum of money for organization purposes.
Another point to which the hon. gentleman alluded was that of the One Big Union. I do not know much of that body and what we hear of it has come to our notice recently, but if it is spoken of as likely to develop socialism in this country, let me tell the hon. gentleman that the policy of the Government is developing another kind of socialism in the shape of the nationalization of all the railways in Canada that they can lay their hands on.
My hon. friend stated that in the years which preceded the advent of the Liberal party to power in 1896 they advocated a policy of free trade, and that as a consequence there was great unrest in the country. The hon. gentleman stated that for forty years previous to that time there had been great progress in industry and in manufactures in Canada and that this was due to the National Policy adopted in 1878. As to that, one thing I can certainly affirm. It is that if industrial development in Canada failed to keep pace with the times it was not due to any policy propounded by the Liberal party, but was due-and nobody can deny it

to the toad administration of the Conservative Government which preceded the advent of the Liberal party to power in 1896. So much dissatisfaction was there with that administration that the lower tariff policy propounded toy the Liberals carried the country in 1896 by a great majority.
My hon. friend has asserted that when the Liberals came into power they made but a slight tariff reduction, and that in the course of fifteen years the reductions only amounted to one and a half per cent. Well, to reduce the tariff at all was a step in the right direction. But the public must have been satisfied with what was done along that line, because when the Liberal Government proposed to go further in 1911, who asked them to move slowly and not go too fast? Who raised the slogan at that time throughout the country, "Let well enough alone?" It was the party of hon. gentlemen opposite.
My hon. friend also says that the policy of the Liberal party on the tariff issue has been one of vote catching and deception. That, Mr. Speaker, has not been the policy of the Liberal party in the years that have passed. Our record is exposed to view for all to see. It is a splendid record and one of which the Liberal party may well be proud. I can assure my hon. friend that if there was a policy of vote catching and deception adopted* by anybody it was adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite. It was, to a large extent, by means of such a policy that they carried the country in 1911. The same policy was followed by them in 1917, and as a result they are in office today. What did they do in 1911? In the province of Ontario they raised the cry that the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier was too much of a Koman Catholic and a Frenchman, whereas in the province of Quebec they went round saying he was too much of an Imperialist. At that time also the Conservatives made an alliance with the Nationalists; they preached a certain policy in Quebec, and they advocated an entirely different policy in Ontario. Was not that in very truth a policy of vote catching and deception?
I wish now to make a few remarks with regard to the subject particularly under discussion, the Budget.
When the Minister of Finance presented his Budget to the House the other day he looked to me like a person who was very much worried; as a man would look who had taken charge cf a beautiful estate that had just been ransajcked by robbers or struck by a tornado. A frenzied and feverish attempt is made to tax every possible source of wealth in a supreme effort to make both ends meet and to repair the damages made by the storm. The Budget, Mr. Speaker, when we look at it, seems to me to be something conceived on the impulse of the moment, not thoroughly thought out as to

detail, its practicability, or its ultimate effect. The Budget is open to serious objection ; in many ways it will increase the cost of living at a time when every person should be trying to reduce it. There is one thing that the Government seems to forget: that the struggle to obtain an adequate share of the necessities of life, even in this country, is becoming, in the case of a vast number of people, a tragedy more than anything else; and it seems to me that the new taxation will increase the struggle rather than diminish it. The Government .seem to have taken as their maxim: "We will tax luxuries in order to check extravagance." That might be a laudable object except for the fact that the only authority the Government have for imposing taxation at all requires them to assess the burden equally upon the whole body of taxpayers and for the exclusive purpose of raising the necessary revenue to carry on the country's affairs. The people, I believe, will resent keenly their being taxed into submission to whatever vhe party in office thinks they should do or should buy, or can afford to pay, and so on.
There are anomalies in the Budget. A suit of clothes is taxed1 at the rate of 10 per cent if it costs $45 or over. Well, I would ask any lion, gentleman if to-day any person can get a decent suit of clothes for $45? It is in very many instances good policy and economy to buy the best clothes, for they last longer. But in view of the new taxation proposals, how many people will be able to afford to do that? Not many. The same thing applies to shoes and other articles which everybody must buy, which nobody can do without. As was said last night by the member for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) the tax cn patent medicine is one which will surely bear heavily on the great masses of the people, because they rely upon these medicines, having not the means to consult a physician or doctor. I. am afraid that in many instances the people will have tc. do without these medicines. Mr. Speaker, calling a tax ''luxury tax" and applying it to staple articles of everyday necessity on the basis of certain prices -the lowest prices at which such articles, of fair quality, can be bought-is simply a bit of camouflage. That is what is involved in this feature of the Budget proposals.
There are other anomalies, Mr. Speaker, in the taxation proposals of the Finance Minister. For instance, pianos, which are purchased chiefly by rich people, are taxed
fMr. Casgrain.]
at 10 per cent, while phonographs, which are commonly used by people of smaller means, are subjected to a tax twice as large. Different opinions have been expressed as to the probable result of the new taxation. The majority of people see in it great disadvantage, increase of cost in operation and a source of trouble to all traders. The method of collecting the taxes on retail transactions is objectionable. It makes the retail merchant an involuntary tax collector and adds to the cost of carrying on his business. It leaves the door open to unscrupulous dealers to ignore the tax or to decline to collect it and make dishonest returns, and it also invites certain non-bona fide dealers to sell at supposedly reduced prices articles of inferior quality, -and in the end it will be the consumer who will once more 'have to pay and bear the burden.
According to the Minister of Finance, our own income tax has not been well applied; the machinery for its collection is imperfect. Well, I Submit with all due .respect that the Minister of Finance should have perfected the machinery for collecting the income tax and should have tried to collect as much under it as possible without resorting to the great majority of the taxes which he has put on to-day and which certainly will bear heavily on the people.
While speaking of income tax, I should like to direct the attention of the minister and of the House generally to another feature of the matter. Why not have the income tax returns made public? Everybody in this country knows what any citizen pays to the municipality, to the school commission, to other public institutions, for taxes; why not make the same thing apply to federal income taxation? Why not make it public that Mr. So-and-so pays $200, $300, $1,000 or $2,000 by way of income tax, in order that the people may know who have made the big money and who ought to be made to pay more?
The country is facing very serious conditions to-day. Canada, like many other countries, is suffering from the effects of post-bellum conditions, although not so acutely as some other countries. In Canada, as in other places-in some instances I would say that the condition is worse in Canada than elsewhere-there has been developing a certain disease which we may call acute profiteering. The amount of wealth in this country has not, I am sure, increased very much during the last decade, but the number of millionaires, Mrt Speaker, as you well know, has increased im-

mensely. The unrest throughout Canada is more pronounced on account oi the increased number of millionaires and the amount of wealth that has been concentrated in the hands of few, while other people who are not mating enough to support themselves find the conditions of living absolutely hard to bear.
Among the new taxes brought down by the Minister of Finance I would like to have seen a tax on land values. Everybody will admit that during the war vacant lands escaped taxation much more than anything else. By the taxing of vacant lands, the country would secure a large income and, in my opinion, the cost of living would be reduced by more adequate facilities being given for building houses, thus relieving housing conditions in different parts of Canada.
I should like to draw the attention of the Minister of Finance to the question of earned and unearned incomes. The income tax, as it stands at present, ought to be modified in such a way that an income, based on sound securities such as real estate, from which the owner will derive great benefit all his life and from which the people who come after him will have an opportunity of being able to live without working, ought to be taxed much higher than an income such as that of a professional man, an industrial expert, an engineer, or any other salaried individual, because that income ceases with the death of the one who earns it; and on account of having to pay the enormous taxes that at present fall on such incomes, a man of this class runs the risk of 'having no capital at all at the time of his death. The man who has a steady income derived from bonds and real estate and who will be able to leave that real estate and those securities to the people who come after him ought to be taxed twice as much as the salaried man. In England, this is done, and it would be well for the Minister of Finance to bear this in mind, and when we get into committee on the resolution, I hope this suggestion will be adopted as part of the legislation.
The Minister of Finance has seen fit to retain for another year the excess business profits tax. I do not agree with him in that regard. He cited a number of reasons why this tax should be abolished, and yet he has retained it. The excess business profits tax has given as much as we can expect from it, because people have got on to it and companies have devised ways and means of hiding their income by expending it in many ways such as advertising or different kinds of improvements, thus making it, in certain cases, impossible for the Government to reach the big institution which make such huge profits.
I desire to take objection to the removal of the tax of 15 per cent on films which are exhibited in moving picture houses. Like most hon. members, I am an amateur at moving picture shows; but I contend that this tax should have been retained for this year, and there is no good reason for its removal. The Minister of Finance gave as a reason for the removal of (this tax the statement that it was bearing 'heavily upon some small institutions, making them pay about 6 or 7 per cent of itheir receipts, whereas big moving picture houses w'ere paying one or two per cent. I have nothing to say against moving picture houses; but I have not yet seen, in any of these theatres, any picture shown that did not in a certain way reflect on morality or come very near to immorality. In many cases, a picture invites luxurious habits and extravagance in expenditure, and this Budget is especially devised to prevent luxury and extravagant expenditure, to curb all these evils. Another point I want to make against these moving picture institutions is that they are responsible, in Montreal, Quebec and other large cities for a great deal of evil that is being committed. In many cases a moving picture show is a common rendezvous for a certain class of people who want to hide themselves. The other day a Montreal judge told me that he bad to pass upon a case of separation, and what happened? The beginning of the case was in a moving picture house. The pictures that are exhibited are suggestive, and in some cases they lead to very bad results. They are an invitation to the people of the poorer classes to revolt, and they bring disorder in the country. Thank 'God, there is not a moving picture show in any town or village in my constituency, and I hope there will not be any for a long time.
I should like to make a few remarks in regard to the tariff, to which a number of hon. gentlemen have referred in this debate. For a long time every person who bestows any thought on our national life has been of the opinion that a change ought to be made in the tariff. Although the Minister of Finance has given us a promise and a declaration of principle as to the commission that is to investigate what the future tariff should be, I am sorry to say that I cannot put much stock in what he has said to us; and for this rea-

importance of these things, he said, that a country could make substantial progress; and let me say, Sir, that it was by a full recognition of the principles so well laid down by His Royal Highness that Canada made such great Strides during the fifteen years of the late Liberal administration.

In common with other hon. members who have spoken, I wish to congratulate the Minister of Finance on the comprehensive and straightforward statement which he has given to the House in regard to our liabilities, and also on the courage which he has displayed in going after sufficient revenue to take care of our responsibilities without resorting 'to further borrowing. I do not intend to take up a great deal of the time of the House, but whatever time I do spend in addressing hon. members I shall devote to a discussion of tariff matters alone. I believe that the tariff is to be the one feature of the next election, and I think it is an important subject at the present moment. Before dealing with this subject, however, I want to refer to a statement made by the hon. member for North Essex (Mr. Kennedy) a few days ago. I am sorry that that hon. gentleman is not in his seat, but I observe that the hon. member for Kent (Mr. McCoig) is present, and the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee), who was here a moment ago is, I regret, absent for the moment. These three hon. gentlemen appear to me to be a sort of co-operative triumvirate from the western part of the province of Ontario. The hon. member for North Essex a few days ago made an attack on the dry dock proposition in the city of St. John, and I must say that he goes a long way from home to make his attack. The hon. member for Kent makes a vicious onslaught on the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Mowat) regarding Massey-Harris and the International Harvester Company, also going far afield; while the other member of the triumvirate attacks the automobile industry. It is interesting to note that there is not an automobile industry in that hon. gentleman's riding, but there is such an industry in the riding of the hon. member for Kent and in the riding of the hon. member for North Essex. He makes his attack upon something that is not a home industry; he takes good care to see to that. Now, I desire to read a statement made by the hon. member for North Essex the other day in his speech. It will be found at page 2730 of unrevised Hansard;

There seems to be an organized plan to raid the public treasury. Now, Canada has done pretty well for the shipbuilding industry, at all events so far as helping them to get started is concerned. X have here a prospectus issued by a bond house dealing with the St. John Dry-dock and Shipbuilding Company, Limited, showing that the Government of Canada have agreed under certain conditions to assist this company to the extent of $247,500 per annum for a period of thirty-five years.
That is going a long way from home to make an attack. I might say, Sir, that this dry dock proposition was inaugurated by a measure passed through this House, and I may read a couple of clauses from the Act incorporating the company. I happen to know something about the establishment of dry docks because I come from ai partly maritime county where we have a dry dock and where, when the Welland Canal is completed, there is likely to be necessity for another dry dock to take care of the larger boats; and when I saw the statement of the hon. member I felt pretty sure that he had either been very much mistaken or that he was misleading the House or trying-to use a vernacular expression-to put something over. Let me read' a couple of clauses from the Act:
The Governor in Council may, as an aid to the construction of any dry dock, authorize the payment out of any unappropriated money forming part of the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada of a subsidy, in accordance with the provisions of this Act, to any incorporated company, approved by the Governor in Council, as having the ability to perform the work, which shall enter into an agreement with His Majesty to construct a dry dock under the provisions of this Act, with all necessary equipment, machinery and plant, for the reception and repairing of vessels.
No such aid shall be granted unless the Governor in Council is satisfied, upon a report of the minister, based upon a report of the Chief Engineer of the Department of Public Works,-
Hon. gentlemen opposite seem to be irritated by It'his expression f' Govternor in Council "; we are always hearing something about it, and so on. This dry dock company, under this law, was established as a public work, and it will be interesting to hon. members to know that the measure establishing it was passed in the year 1910 under the Laurier Government. Hon. members will also see that there were Orders in Council then as well as now, and we are just carrying out the law that was made by the friends of hon. gentlemen opposite. I do not say that the law is a bad one. I think it is good, and those hon. gentlemen are entitled to credit for putting it on the statute book. But I do not see any reason why my hon. friend should have made the

attack which he made, especially when this law was established by his own party. Now the hon. member for Lambton made an attack upon the automobile industry. I do not know that it is my business to defend that particular industry, Mr. Speaker. If there is any one who should defend the automobile industry it would be the hon. member for Kent, in whose city there is a large automobile industry, and the hon. member for North Essex. But they allowed the hon. member for Lambton to come forward and attack this industry by a supposititious case that has no application whatever and no truth at all. That hon. gentleman gives us a supposititious case of an automobile that coat a thousand dollars. Why did not the hon. gentleman get some information from the hon. mem-fer for North Essex or the hon. member for Kent as to the automobile industry if he did not know anything about it? He could have gotten that information if he had sought it.
He could have given it to the House instead of putting on Hansard the statement he did. I wish to correct that statement and to put on Hansard accurate information regarding the automobile industry. I may say for the particular benefit of my hon. friend from Victoria and Carleton (N. B.) (Mr. Caldwell) and other hon. gentlemen who talk about the Ford automobile, that the information I am about to furnish is in reference to that particular car, so that he and his friends may not in future make the same error that they are making now. My figures are based upon prices in effect on the 4th of this month. The hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) told us that any change in price did not amount to a hill of beans, that it was just taking a shirt and collar or a petticoat off some one, so it cannot very much affect my figures.
The Canadian price of the Ford touring car, as far as the Ford Company is concerned-because they have nothing to do with the inland revenue tax that is collected on sales-is $740; the United States price is $575, a difference of $165, or 28 per cent. Now, what I am about to state is not generally known in this country, and although I am not giving this information on the direct authority of the Ford Company, it came to me from an authentic source and I see no reason why it should not be published. It is not generally known that in regard to equipment the car that is put on the United States market by the Ford Company is not on all fours
with the car that- is put on the Canadian market. The Ford Company in this country equip their cars with 34-inch tires, with non-skid treads on the rear wheels, and with demountable rims. The larger-size tires alone are worth $10 more, and the non-skids and demountable rims are worth another $25. In addition, they use a one-man top, finer upholstery, leather door grips, and other accessories that make a difference of $50 more. So that the Canadian Ford car has an equipment costing $85 more than that of the American Ford car. Then there is another factor to be noted. Of course, it is well known that- the Ford Company import certain component parts from their American factories, and the duty on those parts amounts to $23.12. I might say 'that until quite recently none of the automobile companies in this country made all their parts, and even to-day they import a certain proportion of them. There is also a duty on what are termed the unproductive materials that enter into the manufacture of these cars, such as coal, oil, and other articles which do not appear on a car. There is also the item of exchange on the products imported from the other side, and that exchange in the case of the materials that enter into the Ford car amounts to $10.40. Those items total $118.52, leaving a difference between the Canadian Ford car and the United States Ford car of only $48.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that in a business of the proportions of the Ford Company we are very fortunate to have it established in this country even under these circumstances. The reason for that difference of $48 is due to the fact that in the United States the Ford Company turn out 1,000,000 cars as against only 60,000 turned out by the Canadian plant, Therefore the difference in the cost of making the various parts, and in furnishing dies, and other equipment must be plain to every one conversant with modern factory practice. As a matter of fact the Canadian Ford Company have no hesitation in saying that if their business grows-and at present they are exporting
25,000	of the 60,000 cars they manufacture- if their business grows a little more so they can overtake the unit cost of manufacture they will eventually be able to market the Ford car in Canada just as cheaply as in the United States.
It seems to me that it should not be up to me to defend an industry in the county of Kent; certainly I would not want to have another member jump up and do it in respect to an industry in my "own constitu-

ency. But what does this industry mean to Canada in general and to the county in particular in which the hon. member for North Essex lives? Now I want to refer to a book that I have under my hand entitled " The Farmers' Platform." This book was published a year or two ago, but although its colour has not changed, the name, I understand, has, and the Farmers party is now known as the Progressive or the Agrarian party. A year or two ago the old name was good enough, but they were afraid that possibly the class call that was raised against them would be prejudicial to their prospects so they changed their name. I want to refer to several quotations in this book and I wish to do so in a kindly and gentlemanly spirit. I hope that what I shall have to say will be taken in the spirit in which it is inetnded; I do not want to be harsh and I will not .accuse those concerned of profiteering or anything of the kind. The book in question has 
been prepared by the Canadian Council of Agriculture and adopted by the United Farin-ers of Alberta, the Saskatchewan Grain Growers' Association, the Manitoba Grain Growers' Association and the United Farmers of Ontario. It is issued by the Canadian Council of Agriculture and published by the Grain Growers' Guide, so that it is fairly well revised or edited and fairly well, I should think, recommended. The first quotation I shall make is headed, "What the tariff costs," and reads as follows:
As already explained, under a system of protection, the consumer is compelled to pay a tax upon all imported goods that come under the tariff schedule. Upon all goods of domestic origin, produced under a protective system, the consumer must likewise pay a tax-although in this case the revenue finds its way to the bank account of private individuals alone. Now it has been estimated that the domestic trade of Canada alone is at least four times as great as the country's foreign trade, and in the United States seven times as great. It follows that for every dollar collected by way of customs dues, at least $4 are paid to private individuals. When one considers that the customs revenue for the year ending March 31, 1916, was $133,000,000, and that four times that sum was paid in addition to the protected interests, it will be seen what a crushing weight is laid upon the country's consumers.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to avoid all posisibility of a mistake, but this book has been so well edited and revised and so well prepared, that I would not think it pos-ible for a clerical error of any consequence to have crept within its covers. Consequently I am very much surprised to find that the customs revenue for the year ending March 31, 1916, is given as $133,000,000. I now have under my hand the customs returns for that year and they amount to $103,000,000. Of course a difference of thirty millions is only a small item, but you will notice that they say here that the figure is to be multiplied by four as being trade within the country. Thirty millions multiplied by four makes the trifling amount of $120,000,000. I am not advancing this as an argument but merely pointing out that these gentlemen from the Northwest, these new economists who have been studying political economy and all other forms of economy, during the last year, might have paid some attention to the facts, and seen that this book was published in correct form. That would occur to me as a good thing for them to do, and I would recommend that the next time they venture upon such a publication they will see to it that it is accurate. And here I might pause to observe that although in

the first book they issued they went into a lot of particulars they have since learnt a lot of sense; the latest book contains no particulars but simply a lot of glittering generalities-that is all, just generalities.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if the argument is correct that the duty is also collected on all internal trade-that because the internal trade is four times as great as the trade that goes through the custom house then four times the amount of that revenue goes into the pockets of somebody else-I assume that if the internal trade should amount to ten times as much as what comes through the custom house, there would be ten times the amount of duty plundered by somebody-because "plunder" is the word these people use in another case which I shall mention presently. To illustrate the effect of their argument I propose to go through the tariff and mention some of the articles that it contains. First of all I will roughly run through the tariff items that I have marked down; I have not done it very carefully but hurriedly in order to show how absolutely unjust and entirely unreliable any such statement as made here can be. Now out of this $103,-000,000-not $133,000,000 as they say in their book there is the W'ar tax collection and the balance consists of the regular customs returns for that year. But the manufacturers are certainly not interested in the figures that I am going to read, however much other people may be. Consequently if four times, or ten times the amount of taxes have been collected than should have been it cannot be on the items I. am going to read. That will be self-evident as I read them. The first item is-animals, $110,000 duty. Now if there has been $400,000 of duty cribbed by somebody else on this item, you will have to go down into the pockets of some hon. gentlemen sitting on the opposite benches below me and recover that money. The next item is- grain, duty of $400,000. That money was collected on different kinds of grain and if you deduct the exports I assume the grain consumption in the Dominion would be very considerable. Therefore, if it is true that that amount of duty has to be multiplied ten or twelve times I would like to know which hon. member among the Farmers' party has got this money. The next item is $4,000,000 worth of coal. Now the manufacturers cannot be held responsible for that.

The way this is written: "Now, if our contention is sound" would make me believe, Mr. Speaker, that the man who wrote it was not quite sure of his ground; he was not very certain, so he put it that way. From the statement made in the House last year by the member for South Waterloo (Mr. Scott) I am quite convinced that the consumer pays little, if any, duty on the article manufactured in Canada. I am quite convinced that with the keen competition amongst over two hundred manufacturers in this country it would be absolutely impossible for any body of business men carrying on a business of $33,000,000 to make a profit of $10,000,000. What is more, I say to the ' member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) and to the other members of that aggressive party that there is no better field in Canada for a manufacturing enterprise than a proposition built upon that basis; if I were a younger man 1 would get after that business very quickly. Another industry referred to is that reviled industry of canning. Every time some hon. members of this House look around the Chamber you will hear some attack upon the canning industry. Now,
I have something to say about the canning industry. I have in my county over fifteen canning factories, and not half of them are associated with Canners, Limited, either; they are operated by independent concerns, farmers' co-operative and other enterprises. It seems to me that if hon. gentlemen on the other side would ,get together with these men rather than hammer the business, they would make more progress and probably do more to benefit the country than they will ever do by trying to pull them down. It seems to me that there is a class of men running about in this country endeavouring to create class prejudice. There are men who are trying to make the farmer believe that the citizens in the town, his best customer, is his enemy, and others who are trying to make the city man believe that the farmer, his best customer, is his enemy. of the eight or ten manufacturers of tires in this country he will get a tire as cheap as one that is sold in the United States. What I say now has reference to the con-diion of affairs a month or two ago. What prices are to-day I do not know. Rubber and fabric both come from the United States, and the rate of exchange may have altered matters to a slight degree; but under no circumstance is there more than a difference of 5 per cent between the tires made in Canada and those made in the United States.
I have a few lemarks to make in regard to some more goods sold in St. Catharines, and I have personal information in regard to the matters of which I shall speak. I did not want to take figures from any firm in St. Catharines for the purposes of any comparison; I took the trouble to write to a Montreal concern, competitors of mine, who do business in the United States. I do not mind telling the name of the company; it is the Simmonds Saw Company. I got my manager to write and ask what was the selling price in the United States, and in reply we were advised,, "The prices are practically the same." In giving some examples the writer said:
We are selling: such and such a style of saw to mill men in the United States at $5.50 per hundred, and we are selling It in Canada at $5.75 a hundred.
A difference of only 25 cents, or a little more than a postage stamp, especially where we import our raw material. The writer also says:
On mill saws, high grade cross-cut saws, cheap cross-cut saws, points, shanks, etc., there is the same slight difference, and in order that you may have the fullest information which I can give you on American prices, I am attaching discount sheet effective April 1st, 1920, showing the Fitchburg,. Mass, and the Canadian prices.
There is another American firm in my home town, and they write me to say that their largest item of production, malleable iron, is sold just as cheap in Canada as it is in the Unded States.
Then I ha\e a letter from the Yale & Towne Company, a well known concern, also located in St. Catharines, giving me a list of their products,-and I could give a few figures showing their American prices as compared with their Canadian prices, but I will not weary the House with these details. It is sufficient for me to say that the figures show the benefit our people are deriving from these American factories having been established in this country, and that we

are not paying a sou more for tiieir products.
One more item and I have exhausted my list. A firm which manufactures grape juice-a beverage which is very much needed in these dry times-established a factory in my home town, and in reply to my inquiries the manager writes me:
We are selling grape Juice in Canada just as cheap as we are selling it in the United States.
Yet our friends of the Farmers' party would have us believe that tire full tariff is taken by the manufacturers on everything they produce
Before I close 1 want to refer to one other matter which perhaps I should have mentioned before; it is another personal illustration of how the British manufacturer or shipper can be protected without a tariff. Not very long ago my company was enjoying business at the coast on a certain article, and suddenly that business dropped off, our agent advising us that the decline was owing to some British goods coming in- We know that the British trader as a rule does not cut prices, and in that respect he is not like his brother in the United States; the British trader makes his prices out of the freight rates and his lower cost of manufacture, and very seldom does he cut prices. We applied to our Liverpool agents to ascertain what the rate of freight was from Liverpool to Victoria, B.C., and we discovered that the Canadian Pacific Railway was carrying the goods from Liverpool across this continent at $1.25 per hundred freight. Our freight rate from the factories at St. Catharines to the same point on the identical class of goods was $1.80. In other words, the difference in the rate was a profit in itself I appealed to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, because it looked to me like an outrage, but I got no satisfaction Then a body of our manufacturers got together in Montreal, and from our plant there we shipped those goods down to Vera Cruz in Mexico and across Mexico up the Coast and landed them in Victoria at 90 cents a hundred. It was not until we were able to protect ourselves in that way that we could deal with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. Then they came to us and quoted us a rate of $1 a hundred, which enabled us to hold that trade. I just mention that to show that there are other factors besides the tariff to protect a manufacturer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am through. I merely want to add that I come from a
county that has had a wonderful expansion in manufactures, and I ask the people of this 'ountry if their representatives here are going to do something which will injure that industrial prosperity. I come from a county that has spent on its fruit industry millions of dollars; and tho.se fruit farmers want the duty on fruit retained. Gentlemen cf the Farmers party may talk as much as they like, but the fact remains that the people in my county want that tariff, and if my friends of the Farmers party will go dowm there they will find out the real state of affaires in pretty quick time. Again I ask hon. gentlemen: What are you going to do? Are you goin to do something that will destroy these industries?
I am rather ashamed, Mr. Speaker, at having taken up so much of the time of the House, but I have the excuse that I have not transgressed very much before. I wish to thanv hon. members very heartily for the kind atention that they have given to me remarks.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton (N.B.):
subtopic: DEBATE CONTINUED ON THE ANNUAL STATEMENT PRESENTED BY THE MINISTER OF FINANCE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding to discuss the Budget and the amendment to it which is before the House, I would like to deal briefly with some of the remarks made by the last speaker, the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Chaplin). Especially do I want to deal with his statement with regard to the difference in the American and the Canadian price of a Ford car. And when I speak on this matter I am not speaking of something that some one told me or that some one wrote to me; I am speaking from personal experience.
In the early stages of this session I made a statement in regard to this matter, and I might say that the hon. member for Lincoln was not the only person who got up in the air about it. Here is a letter I received from the manager of the Ford Motor Company, covering four large Sheets of paper, as the House will observe. In it he advances much the same argument as that employed by the hon. member for Lincoln, and he even threatened that he would put this in the hands of some hon. member and that I would get a " trimming." Well, I am quite prepared to take a " trimming " when it is coming to me, but it is not coming this time, thank the Lord! I want to quote some of the contents of this letter, and then I will come to the facts. The manager of the Ford, Company wrote:

In the case of the Ford touring car-which is the article which is the major proportion of our production-I may say that the equipment of the Canadian car is somewhat different from that of the car in the United States. Inasmuch as we put on larger tires and the car is also equipped with demountable rims and extra tire carrier and other items of this kind, which makes the car in Canada of considerably more monetary value.
Further on he says:
We put on a one-man top and a ventilating wind shield also.
I have worn out one Ford car. In September last I bought another one, and I have the receipted bill right here, the items of which I will give a little later. I bought this car in Woodstock, N.B. I was in the town of Holton, in the state of Maine, only twelve miles from Woodstock, the day before I bought the car. I priced the value of the car in Holton. I will admit there was a difference in the forward tires. The forward tires on the Ford car in Maine are three inches whereas in the case of the Ford car sold in New Brunswick those tires are three and a half inches, representing a difference in the neighbourhood of $7 in price. In all other respects the car was exactly the same as the car I bought in Woodstock the next day. The car I bought did not have the one-man top, or a ventilating wind shield, or demountable rims or have even a tool box or tire carrier; the only difference was in regard to the forward tires. The car I bought has a self-starter which is identical with the self-starter made by the same firm in the case of the Holton car. With regard to the starter the difference in the price was $40. This starter cost $70 in Holton whereas in Woodstock it cost $110, a difference of $40 on a $70 article notwithstanding the fact that the hon. gentleman who has just	taken	his	seat told	us	thatmanufactured	goods	are	as cheap	in	Canada as they are in the United States notwithstanding the duty.

If the hon. member
will have the patience to listen what I am stating may penetrate his cranium if it is not too thick, before I have done. Now the car I bought	cost $900, and	thetire carrier	$7.25,	a	total of	$907.25
for the, bare car without any tool box to carry tools in. Even without any tire carrier the car cost $900 in Woodstock when I could have bought it for $640 in Holton. Allowing for $7 on account of the

difference in the tires that would make the Holton car $253 cheaper. I said to the dealer in Woodstock " I should have bought a car in Holton yesterday, I could have bought one for $240 less." He replied "Yes, but the car would cost you just the same when you brought it in because you would have had to pay duty on it." It was because of the duty I was charged the extra $240 in Woodstock, and in these purchases we cannot help ourselves. There has been a campaign conducted in Canada for the last few years-you will see the posters on every fence, and on every vacant lot-urging you to buy " Made in Canada goods " otherwise you are a traitor to your country. If I had bought this car in Holton I would have got it for $240 less and would have paid $240 in duty on it, and I consider that I would have been more patriotic to my country because then the revenue of Canada would have benefited to the extent of $240 instead of it going into the manufacturer's pocket.
The hon. member for Lincoln made the statement that there was a duty of twenty cents a bushel on potatoes. I did not quite catch the whole of his remark in that oon-' neetion and I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not at present in the Chamber. If he were here I would ask him if that applied to potatoes going out of or coming into Canada. I want to tell him that he does not know what he is talking about, there is no duty on potatoes going from Canada to the United States or on potatoes coming from the United States into Canada. He also states that there were 20,000,000 bushels exported I can prove that he is wrong in that statement because we have never exported more than 4,150,000 bushels from Canada in any one year according to the export statistics:
It would also be of interest to the House, it would certainly be of interest to the people of Canada, to know that the hon. gentleman-who by the way just made the kind of speech I would expect him to make after looking up, shall I call it his pedigree, in the Parliamentary Guide-is the president of two large manufacturing firms therefore he delivered just the kind of speech I would expect such a man to make.
I do not blame him much because if the Farmers' platform is put into effect-to call it by its right name, which he seems *to think we are ashamed of, but we are not-he and his like will certainly lose a nighty good graft they are collecting off the people of Canada.

The hon. gentleman also said he would like to discuss the Farmers' platform throughout the country. Mr. Speaker, I think you wild admit that the discussion of the Farmers' platform has so far not brought very good results to the party the hon. gentleman supports. That platform has been discussed not by the farmers alone but by others. In the recent by-elections we had the spectacle of some of the ablest ministers in the present Cabinet going out and discussing the features of that platform. If they were not able to present it in a way that would make the people condemn it, that fact is surely a commendation of our platform.
Another thing the hon. member said was that the gross difference in the price of a Ford car in the United States amounted to $165. He worked that down, I believe, to $48. The manager of the Ford Motor Car company claimed that there is a difference of $130 between the American car and the Canadian oar. Therefore he could not have written the same letter to the hon. member for Lincoln that he wrote to me, and I have the bill of the car I bought, under the Ford Motor Company's own bill heads, at $900 without even the tire-holder or tool box. The House will believe me when I make this statement and I am not saying something that somebody wrote me or telegraphed me. As I say I bought this car and paid $240 more for it on account of buying it in Canada instead of the United States. They tell you, Mr. Speaker, that the experience you buy is the best experience you can get if it does not cost you too much. I feel that my experience in this case cost just a little too much.
I had not the privilege-on account of illness in my family-of being in the House when the Budget Speech was delivered. Perhaps I was more disappointed than surprised to find that no provision was made for a revision of the tariff, although we were promised last year that the whole tariff question would be investigated before the present session was called so that the Government could deal with it intelligently. The ex-Finance Minister (Sir Thomas White) in the Budget Speech which he delivered on June 5, 1919, is reported as making the following promise:
It is my hope that within a year conditions will have become so stabilized as to permit of a general revision of the tariff, which is- long, but, owing to the war, unavoidably overdue. Preceding such revision there should be a thorough inquiry conducted by the Minister of Finance and two or more of his colleagues representing the different geographical sections of Canada. Such inquiry should afford all interests, agricultural, industrial, fishing, lumbering, mining, commercial, and financial, producers and consumers alike, an opportunity of expressing their views and opinions and urging their particular needs and requirements. The rsult of such inquiry should be a body of information which will enable the Government to effect a general revision of the tariff fair to all parts of the community, and effectually promoting the national welfare of Canada. This inquiry should proceed with its work just as soon as conditions are sufficiently stabilized to permit. My own view is that it might well be commenced about autumn of this year.
That was in 1919. And yet we had the spectacle in this House recently of the Finance Minister (Sir Henry Drayton) bringing down his Budget and promising that there shall be a revision some time in the dim and distant future. The ex-Finance Minister said that t-his revision was overdue a year ago, or almost a year ago. If it was overdue at that time it is certainly more than overdue to-day. I think we have a right to be disappointed to find that no mention is made of the revision of the tariff this year; the Government speak of waiting until the conditions are stabilized. I think, Mr. Speaker, that considering the course the present Government are taking the conditions will be no more stabilized than they are to-day until we have a general election and perhaps a change of Govem-menU-who knows? I think the low tariff supporters of the Government must be easily satisfied if this continued promise of revision from year to year satisfies them. However, I was glad to notice yesterday that they are not all satisfied; that some of them have the courage of their convictions, the courage to get on their feet and condemn the party which they have supported, when they believe it is wrong. If the Government are wise they will take warning from the defections from their ranks, made by men who have supported them for years.
I would warn the Government also not to put off too long this promised investigation into the tariff, because if they put it off a couple of years or more they man not have the opportunity of making the investigation. If they wish to investigate tariff conditions and adopt a tariff that will be satisfactory to Canada, they are making a great mistake, if I may be allowed to give them that advice, in putting it off as long as they have. Their chances for re-election would have been much better if they had brought down a measure for reduction of the tariff this year.
I am very much pleased to see the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) in his seat; I thought that he was going to leave the Chamber, and I wanted to direct his

attention to one or two matters. I was rather amused at his speech the other evening, and he is not usually amusing. I do not think that he really meant to be amusing on this occasion, because he seemed to be in his usual sarcastic form. Shall I be allowed to say that he even seemed to be a bit anxious? In one breath he said that it would be the ruination of Canada to lower the tariff, and in the next breath he claimed credit for the party he supports for lowering the tariff on a number of articles, and for taking off the 7i per cent special war tax.

He did not explain to this House or to the country that the present Government put on this 7f per cent duty in the first place; yet he brags that the Government took it off. The minister's reduction of the tariff reminds me very much of this kind of cheap sale.
Another statement the Minister of the Interior made the other evening was that he thought the new Progressive party should support the party in this House that acted, not a party which only professed and did not act on those professions. He also made a great ado because we did not move the Farmers' platform as an amendment to the Budget. Now, no man in this House knows better than the Minister of the Interior that the rules of this House allow only one amendment to be moved to the Budget. The fact that the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) was the first speaker after the Budget was delivered and that he moved his amendment before he sat down effectively shut us out from moving any other amendment. But, in the first place, I wish to state that the new Progressive party do not propose to support either party in this House.

speechtext:
Thank you; no doubt we will do dt. I have no doubt that the Government will adopt that platform after the discussion is over. I notice that it seems to be in great demand among the supporters of the Government and that they have already adopted some of its best 'features. If they should be lucky enough to hold on to office by hook or by crook, I think that they will adbpt it all.
But, as I say, we do not propose to support either of the old parties in this House. When a question arises such as the present question before the House we intend to take a stand on it that will be in the best interests of Canada. We may err, but if we do we shall err in judgment; we shall not be whipped into line to support this party or that against our convictions,-do not make any mistake about that. I think that we have proved our independence in this House during the present session; we have voted with the Government perhaps as often as against them. I am only sorry that we were not able to vote with them oftener, because if we had been able to vote with them it would have meant that they were bringing down good legislation, legislation for the good of Canada and which we would have been pleased to support. We do not come here to oppose any party; we are not like the Irishman who said: "Is there a government in the country?" and upon receiving a reply in the affirmative, said: "Well, I am opposed to it." We are certainly not in that position. We are here to support good legislation, not party. Partyism is what has brought governments in Canada-and I use the word "governments" advisedly-to such a condition as that which we see to-day. When people support a party regardless of how-d am almost at a loss for a word to express it strongly enough without disobeying the rules of the House-regardless of how much evil they have committed and how bad the administration is, it tends to bad government. The indications are that this Government will be turned down, if the late by-elections are any indication of the feeling of the people in constituencies where opinion was formerly pretty well divided as-between the two parties. I think the Government themselves realize what that means.
With regard to the amendment that is before us, I for one do not approve it in its entirety. But I shall certainly support the amendment, because we have been denied by the rules of the House the privilege of moving a second amendment and I consider

the amendment is the lesser of two evils. I would like very much, however, to see the third party in this House recognized as such, so that we should have the privilege of moving a second amendment. When there were only two parties in this House it was certainly proper that there should be only one amendment moved to the Budget, but ,when there are three parties it is no more than right and fair that two parties should have the privilege of moving amendments. However, we do not feel like insisting very strongly upon our rights as a third party, because we do not expect always to occupy third place in this House. I do not think any hon. member who is in touch with the feeling of the people would be considered a prophet if he expressed the view that after the next general election the present Government would be occupying third place in this House-I am not a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, but I am not afraid to make this prophecy-and those who live to see will know-that the Unionist party will be the smallest party in this House after the next general election. I firmly believe that, and, as an hon. gentleman near me says, I think the Government believe it too.

Now, the new system of taxation as proposed by the Finance Minister is said to be a luxury tax on manufacturers and wholesalers, but, to my mind, if that is the mark aimed at, the minister has missed it by a considerable distance. The maximum price on articles exempt from this tax is too low. The poorer, a man is the less, for instance, he can afford to buy shoes under $9 a pair, because the cheaper shoes are not of good quality and not good value for the money. What applies to shoes also applies to clothes. No man knows better than the Finance Minister that you cannot buy a decent suit of clothes at less than $45, the maximum price of an untaxed suit. If the maximum amount exempted had been half as much again, it would have been nearer the mark. On the other hand, instead of taxing the manufacturer and wholesaler, the Government are simply imposing .another tax on the. consumer, because the manufacturer adds the amounf of these taxes to his invoices. In fact, the Minister of Finance has instructed him to do so; on Hansard, unrevised edition, page 2571, the manufacturer is specially instructed not to include the tax in the price of the goods but to
invoice the goods at the factory price and to state the amount of the tax as a separate item on the invoice. Therefore, the Minister of Finance, by no stretch of his imagination, could claim that this was a tax on the manufacturer, because the manufacturer was instructed to pass it along and mark it as a separate item on the invoice.
I notice the Minister of Finance, as reported on page 2571 of unrevised Hansard, states that this tax shall be deemed to have come into force on the 19th day of May, 1920. I do not know what time of the day these resolutions were presented, but I understand they were presented one afternoon and put into effect the next morning. If this be the case, if the minister can draft a Bill and present it to this House one afternoon and have it put into force the next morning, what is the need of calling Parliament together at all? I had thought that a Bill had to pass this House by a majority of votes and after that be ratified by the Senate, and be signed by the Governor General before it became law. 0.f course, we know thalt the present Administration has set all kinds of precedents by way of Orders in Council, but it certainly gave me quite a jolt to find that the Finance Minister could enact a law overnight, and put it into effect the next morning before breakfast. Truly the day of miracles is coming back to us again. It would be much quicker, instead of calling Parliament, for the Minister of Finance to handle this end of the matter; the Minister of the Interior could handle his department, and so on. The trouble is that the Government have not sufficient ministers to man all the departments, and they dare not appoint any new ministers and send them out for election because they might not come back; they might get lost. I might, however, suggest to the Minister of Finance a source of revenue that would not impose a hardship on the common people of Canada; in fact, I believe it would confer a benefit on them. My suggestion would be to impose an export duty on our print paper, say of 10 per cent. I believe there is a possibility that hundreds of our small papers will go out of business after July 1, because at that time their contracts for newsprint, I understand, will expire, and the cost of paper at the present time is so great that the small papers, without increasing their subscriptions to a price that their subscribers would not, perhaps, feel like paying for the paper, will not be able to carry on.
This may not appeal'to the Government because, perhaps, the Government would

be pleased if there were fewer newspapers printed dn this country; Perhaps they would be as well pleased if the doings in this House, especially an event that happened on the other side of the House last night, were not heralded broadcast in the newspapers of this country. I saw this big headline in the newspapers this morning: "Big defection from the Government ranks last night." No doubt the Government would have been pleased if that had not appeared. I believe the United States' papers are willing to pay per ton for newsprint $240, in American money, which means much mors in Canadian money at the present time. I believe the representative of a number of British dailies is in Canada, and he has $40,000,000 with which to buy what newsprint he can pick up. If there were a 10 per cent export duty on this commodity, we would collect $4,000,000 on this one deal. I believe there is also in Canada a Hindoo who represents a large combination of publishers in Bombay and who has power to purchase newsprint, price being no consideration, and he wants newsprint is thousand-ton lots. Two years ago, our publishers were paying $45 a ton for newsprint; after the 1st of July they expect to be compelled to pay $240 a ton. Of course, our publishers are not objecting so much to- the price; their fear is that they may not be able to secure a supply at all, because these outside firms are willing to pay almost any price for the full output of Canadian newsprint. If I might be allowed, as a new member, to make a suggestion to a gentleman so high up as the Minister o-f Finance, I would suggest that he take this into his serious consideration.

Of course the same
old cry will be raised, how will you raise your revenue? I should like to ask my high protectionist friends how the revenue has always been raised. The people of Canada must always raise the revenue, but there has been a tendency for the party in power in this country to. make the people believe that the Government by some miraculous agency was able to raise the revenue of the country without going into the pockets of the people. It is up to this Parliament (and wei can all assist if they will take our aflvice a little) ,to devise the most economic method
(Mr. Caldwell.]
for raising the revenue. I do not think a man needs to be any very great student of economics to realize that our present tariff is the most extravagant method of raising the revenue that could be devised, for, as I have shown, pretty clearly I think, for every dollar of duty, especially on the implements of production which I have mentioned, that goes into the treasury of the country, perhaps three or four go into the pockets of the Canadian manufacturer, or worse still, into the pockets of the American manufacturer with a Canadian branch factory, who sends the duty he collects from the Canadian people back to his Yankee bank account.

Undoubtedly. I do
not blame the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, or the hon. member for Lincoln for protesting against the lowering of the tariff, because it would cut off a mighty nice graft they have been collecting from the people. I put the blame where it rightly belongs, and that is on the shoulders of any government or any party in this country which will enaot legislation allowing them to do this. The Canadian Manufacturers' Association, or its members, are only human after all-we are all more or less human. One of these Canadian manufacturers is so human that I think he made the statement under oath that he was not running his factory for the glory of God, but to make dividends for the shareholders. That is what we are all doing more or less, but I hope -that some of us, in our daily work and business, are giving a little more glory to God than that man was. However, I say I do not blame these people, but the Government, which enacts legislation which enables them to do it, and even instructs them through that legislation how to do it by stating on the invoice to the next man to whom the manufacturer sells his goods what the tax is and to charge it up, for fear it would not otherwise be charged up to the retailer, and in turn to the consumer. From my experience with the manufacturers I do not think those instructions were needed. I do not think the Minister of Finance needed ito add that rider to his Bill.
Of course, your high protectionists will say that if you take the duties off these things, it means direct taxation. I for one, am not afraid of direct taxation, nor are the farmers of this country, and if the farmers, the largest property holders in

Canada-I say that without fear of successful contradiction-are not afraid of direct taxation, why should the resit of the people be afraid of it? I consider that direct taxation is the only equitable method of raising the revenue, because then every man in Canada will pay his share according to his ability to pay. In other words, he pays according to what he is worth, instead of on what he consumes. I think the tariff carried to its logical conclusion even tends to race suicide in this country, aud I will show you why. You need not laugh Mr. Cockshutt, because I can show you that what I say is true.
