speechtext:
I do not mind the laugh, Mr. Speaker, and I know it does the member for Brantford good. By direct taxation a man is taxed on what he is worth and not on what he consumes. I believe, Sir, that the tariff, carried to its logical conclusion will tend to race suicide at the present high cost of living. Take a labouring man working for ordinary wages and having to support a family of nine; indeed, Mr. Speaker, I know a man in my constituency-he is a farmer-with a family of twenty-one. At the present high cost of living, with the high duty on woollen goods and shoes, and with this new tax added to all these articles if they come above the maximum price at which goods are exempt-and I believe that a good many articles will come above that price even when bought by the poorest people in Canada-it will be almost prohibitive for a poor man to raise a family. For that reason I think I am justified in saying that the tariff will tend to race suicide; I think I am logical in that statement. With regard to direct taxation I am very much pleased to know that I am in such close accord, on this very important subject, with one of the oldest and possibly one of the wisest parliamentarians in Canada to-day. I refer to the hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster), and I
desire to quote from his speech delivered on May 18, 1920, at page 2592 of unrevised Hansard:
Every one must realize the tact that there is a duty to be done, and that it is not by the indirect method that it shall be done. We have had two systems of taxation, one almost entirely predominating up to the present time, and that is the method of indirect taxation, by which the people paid heavily and did not know when they were doing so. All sorts of assertions have been made as to the amounts they paid1,-assertions which of course would partake of the particular power of imagination of the man who made them and of his boldness of speech. All kinds of assertions, have been made, many of them grotesquely exaggerated; but nevertheless one of the features of indirect taxation is that you pay out not knowing how much you do pay. I doubt if that system of taxation altogether imposed upon a country is a good school teacher to that country, and does finally eventuate in what is best for the interests of the people.
To draw a comparison, Mr. Speaker, or to illustrate the principle of indirect taxation I might suggest that it is just the same as if a storekeeper, when a customer went into his store to buy something, got some one to divert that person's attention while he picked his pockets, and if the customer did not know that this was being done it would be all right, That is the principle of indirect taxation carried to its logical conclusion : " If you do not know that your money is gone, therefore it is not gone." The statement I have just quoted, coming from an hon. gentleman of the ability and experience of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, a man who has always advocated the indirect method of raising a revenue-or in other words a tariff for revenue-cannot fail to impress the members of this House and the people of this country.
I wish also, before I sit down, to compliment the hon. Minister of Finance on the fact that he had the courage to say that he would not exempt the last Victory loan from taxation, especially in view of the precedent which his predecessor had established in the matter. I wish also to compliment the Government on the enactment of the income tax measure, as I believe it is one of the wisest acts that have been passed by this Government, and I also believe that the exemption of the former Victory loans was perhaps the most- unwise act of the present Administration. I think, -Mr. Speaker, that " unwise " is even too mild a word to express my disapproval of this act, and I hardly think the ex-Minister of Finance realized the seriousness of this act at the time, nor the far-reaching consequences of it. In the first place, now that we have this very wise income tax Act,

the people with large incomes are seeking every avenue of escape from its operation, and this exemption of the Victory bonds provides a very good way of escape for them. And in view of the immense revenue that Canada must raise, not only this year, hut for at least as long a period or possibly longer, than these bonds are issued for, I consider it was little short of criminal to exempt them from taxation, for in this way our wealthy men in Canada are able to tie up their wealth so that we cannot tax the income from it, and the Government know what that means; at any rate I hope they do. It means that if the wealth of the country escapes taxation, the rest of us must pay more in consequence.
Last summer as I travelled through the province from which I come I saw in every broker's window, and in the windows of a good many barristers in the different towns through which I passed, some such notice as this: ''Victory bonds bought and sold"; and I wondered what they meant, because I knew there was no Victory loan floated at that time. My mother used to tell me when I was a boy that I was of a rather inquisitive turn of mind, and I fear that I have not entirely overcome that failing, if it is a failing. I was therefore somewhat curious to know what this notice meant. On inquiry I found that they were not selling Victory bonds at all but were buying them, and I was anxious to know the reason. The corporations and individuals in our .province-and T imagine that what is true in the case of New Brunswick it true in regard to every other province in Canada-who formerly had money to loan on real estate were withdrawing fit as fact as they could find tax-exempt bonds to .invest in. They were withdrawing their money out of these loans as fast as possible and getting different brokers and barristers to buy Victory bonds. Someone will say, perhaps, that they would not get many. Well, Sir, it would surprise you to know how many they gathered in. We have many patriotic .people in our province, and though I would not claim a greater share of patriotism for that province than exists in any other province, I do not think that it will take second place to any other part of Canada so far as response to duty is concerned. We have a number of very patriotic people in our province, I say, who did not have very much money to invest but who felt that they should do what they could to help in the crisis that faced the country. A number of these people bought Victory bonds and made a payment down of only 
10 per cent. At a later period they were having a hard time to finance their business, or for one reason or another they were not able to make their further payments, either it was not convenient for them to do so, or they could make more money perhaps in some other avenue of business; at any rate, a large number of these small bond holders-not the big ones, but holders' of $50, $100, and $500 bonds -were anxious to 'sell, and the brokers gathered up their bonds. The consequence is that in New Brunswick to-day you cannot borrow money on real estate at the same interest that you could before those Victory loans were floated. It not only deprives the people of this wealth in New Brunswick, as well as all over Canada, but it makes it harder for the poor man who wants to get into business to borrow money; so it has had a double effect.
Another thing that makes the tax exemption of these bonds more iniquitous than an ordinary Act of Parliament is the fact that it cannot be repealed; it is like the laws of the Medes and Persians. Being a part of the agreement made with the people of Canada when we borrowed this money from them, no .Government has any power to rescind or vary it, and we must stand toy that agreement, no matter how iniquitous we find it to be.
I wash also to refer to another matter, contained in a series of questions that I put on the Order Paper and which were answered on March 16 by the Minister of Railways (iMr. Reid)-and I am very sorry that he is not in his seat. However, he will be able to read this in Hansard and I hope he will be able to clear the matter up for me, because I must confess that it has disturbed me somewhat. The questions are as follows:
Did) the Dominion Government make an. agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to secure running rights for the said St. John and Quebec Railway trains over the said Canadian Pacific railway between Westfield Beach and St. John?
The answer is: No. The next question is:
If so, what was the date of such agreement and the terms?
The answer is: Answered by No. 4. The next question is:
And if the Dominion Government did not make such agreement, who did, and what are the terms?
The answer is:
St. John and Quebec Railway Co. The terms are as follows: St. John and Quebec Railway Co.

are to pay interest on a proportion of the value of the joint section plus a proportion of all working expenses calculated on a wheeiage basis.
The last question is:
Is the Dominion Government now operating the St. John and Quebec Railway as part of the Dominion Government railway system?
The answer to which ie:
This line is being operated by the Canadian Government railways as part of the system.
Those answers look all right on their face, but I was afraid at the time that possibly the Minister of Railways did not have correct information, for I did not suppose the error was a typographical one and knowing the facts in connection with this transaction I realized these answers could not be correct. Consequently I was not at all surprised when I saw the statement made by the Premier of New Brunswick in the Provincial House of Assembly on April 19, 1920, in regard to this matter. It will be noticed that the answers to my questions were given on the 16th of April, and the Premier of New Brunswick made his statement three days later. He said:
It was expected that the Canadian National railways would take over the road for operation when completed on September 1st, 1919u For more than a year previous the directors of the company had been urging on the management of the Canadian National railways the necessity of making some arrangement with the Canadian Pacific railway for running rights between St. John and Westfield. Assurance had been given by the officials of the Canadian National railways that such arrangements had been made and that there would be no difficulty or delay. When the road was completed, however, it was found that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company would not allow Valley railway trains to run over their tracks until an agreement in writing had been made. The statute provided that if the St. John and Quebec Railway Company did not make an arrangement for running rights that the Canadian National railways could do so, in which case the Valley railway could take no share of the receipts from the line between Westfield and St. John, nor would it be obliged to pay the rental and other charges in respect to that section. The Canadian National Railway people had due notice that the province would not assume the burden of paying the Canadian Pacific railway for running rights. It was felt that the interest on the money borrowed for the purpose of constructing the railway entailed a sufficient burden for the people of New Brunswick and it would not be wise to assume additional obligation, a rental which apparently would have amounted to $100,000 per year. They thought that the Dominion, which had done so much to relieve other provinces in railway matters, could very easily take up the responsibility of providing for the connecting link between Westfield and St. John, The Government of New Brunswick and the directors had been active in seeing to it that an agreement between the Canadian National
railways and the Canadian Pacific railway was consummated, and after considerable delay the Valley railway trains were allowed to run into St. John. The delay was regrettable, and the Government of New Brunswick felt that it was . attributable to the officials of the Canadian National railways and not to the directors of the St. John and Quebec Railway Company or the Provincial Government. Neither the Government of New Brunswick nor the railway company has agreed to be bound by any arrangement with respect to running rights, nor had the Canadian National railways been authorized to act on behalf of the Government of New Brunswick in connection therewith. The Government of New Brunswick did not expect to receive any portion of the receipts for the section between St. John and Westfield.
That is a copy of the official report of the statement made toy the Premier of New Brunswick. It will he readily seen that if the answers of the Minister of Railways are correct, this statement is not correct; while if the statement toy the Premier of New Brunswick is correct, the answers toy the Minister of Railways to my questions are not correct. I hope that when the railway Estimates are before the House the Minister of Railways will clear up this matter, because it is of some concern to our province.
I believe that the Canadian Pacific Railway proposition was that the Government should pay 6 per cent on half the cost of the ten mile section from Westfield Beach to St. John, valued at $3,000,000. That would amount to $90,000 per year. Besides that the Government were to pay a proportion of all the working expenses calculated on a wheeiage basis, which would amount, as the Premier of New Brunswick has said, to $100,000 or more. Perhaps this will give us some insight into why the Canadian National railways made a deficit last year of $47,000,000, for if the system is managed by the same inefficient methods as the running rights were secured by, it is no wonder that we have such a heavy deficit.
The gross earnings of this St. John and Quebec railroad for the five months from October 31, 1918, to March 31, 1919, were $31,505.08. At that rate they would amount to $75,612.12 per annum. For the further period of six months from March 31, 1919, to September 30, 1919, the gross earnings were $24,873.08, or at the rate of $49,746.12 per annum. For the four years that the railway has been in operation, from April 1, 1915, to March 31, 1919, the total gross earnings were $145,121.45. So it will be readily seen that if the management of the Canadian National railways has to pay the Canadian Pacific Railway Company $100,000 yearly for running rights

over ten miles of road, -when the traffic over the whole road for which they want those running rights will only earn at best $49,746 per annum, it would take over four years to earn the money to pay for the running rights over this ten mile section for one year. Surely this is poor business.
The criticism I have to offer, Mr. Speaker, is this: When this road was first contemplated it was proposed to build it so as to connect with the Transcontinental at Grand Falls and with the Intercolonial system at St. John. But unfortunately this railroad has been made a political football from its inception. If the road had been built as it was first intended from Grand Falls to St. John it would have been competing with the Canadian Pacific between these two points. I W'ould not like to say that the Canadian Pacific held this project up, but there have been some sinister influences at werk ever since the line was first surveyed and construction begun. Instead of beginning at one end they began construction in the middle; they built in both directions and have not got to either end yet, although it has been under construction and partly in operation for four years. It still lacks some forty miles of connecting with the Transcontinental at Grand Falls and it lacks the necessary ten miles that would give it connection with the Intercolonial at St. John. However, my criticism in connection with the securing of these running rights is that the management of the Canadian National rai1 ways did not endeavour-it would seem from the statement of the premier of New Brunswick -to secure running rights over the Canadian Pacific until the road was completed and trains were being operated. I know for a fact that trains were operated to Westfield on the St. John and Quebec railway for nearly a week before the Canadian Pacific would allow their train to run into St. John over this road because the arrangements had not been made. According to the Premier of the province of New Brunswick if the management of the Canadian National railways had endeavoured, before the road was completed, to secure running rights from the Canadian Pacific according to its agreement they would have obtained those running rights at that time and would have got much Setter terms from that company, because they could have said "Why, your terms do not suit us. We can build that ten mile section and the interest on the cost of construction yearly will not be more than it would cost us for running rights.

We will build to St. John and compete with you." If they had taken that stand the cost involved to the country would have been less than $100,000 yearly. That is the criticism I have to offer on the subject of not securing running rights for this road, because I am informed on credible authority that no agreement has yet been signed with the Canadian Pacific. If I am wrong the Minister of Railways will be able to correct me ana I will be pleased to submit to his correction. I asked for the production of all the papers and correspondence in connection with this matter some time ago, and although I was promised them they have not yet been brought down. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that whoever is responsible for the carrying out of this promise will see that I get those papers, and I hope that the Minister of Railways, when the railway estimates are before the House, will furnish Parliament and the country with the information in answer to the statement of the Premier of New Brunswick.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have already taken up more time than I expected to, but there is still another matter that I would like to npeak on.
An lion. MEMBER: Carried.

speechtext:
No doubt hon. members opposite would like me to cease from further remarks because I do not think they have been at all enjoying what I have been saying. I would like to dwell for a few moments on the attitude of hon. members opposite towards the farmers of Canada. They have not missed an opportunity to belittle the farmers or the men who were elected on the Farmers' platform-if you care to call it that. We think that the new Progressive party sounds a little better. Still we are not ashamed of the Farmers' platform; it is a good platform, it is a platform that was promulgated by the men who feed you all.
On more than one occasion hon. gentlemen opposite have accused the farmers of being profiteers. Not to be partial with my favours, I would say that members of the Liberal party have also accused us of being profiteers-although not as often or as- severely as members on the Government side have done. There has been a great deal said about the present high cost of potatoes in Canada or, to be more correct the high cost of potatoes during the last six weeks or two months. Now I desire to give the House a little inside information as to the reason for the high cost of potatoes.

I would like also to state that the potato growers of Canada have not benefited very much by the high cost of potatoes during the last few months for the simple reason that they had none to sell. I think I will be able to prove this to you before I have concluded my remarks. However I want to indulge in a little retrospect before I do that. In 1918 the Union Government instituted a "Greater Production Campaign" and it was one of the wisest things they ever did. I may say I was a member of the Greater Production Committee for our province. I think perhaps I spent as much time as any one individual in New Brunswick in advocating greater production. I attended a number of meetings with the speaker whom the Government paid a good salary for his work. I did not get any salary or any expenses-I did not want any. I also assisted at a number of these meetings. However, I want to tell you that the speaker I have referred to was doubtless as good a man as the Government could have got in New Brunswick-I refer to Professor Keirstead, of the university of New Brunswick. The Government could not have secured a better man for the purpose and he did his work well. Our farmers responded nobly to that appeal. Being potato growers largely in New Brunswick" and not wheat growers, our farmers increased their acreage of potatoes, perhaps forty per cent that year, but, due to adverse weather conditions and the poor grade of fertilizer we got, we were not able to secure as good results as were hoped for. We were not able to get any of the Alsatian potash at all. Now any man who is familiar with potato growing knows that potash is one of the essential plant foods for potatoes. Before the war we were able to get fertilizer, containing ten per cent of Alsatian potash, at $36 per ton. In 1918 some of the fertilizer we were able to obtain, without the ten per cent of Alsatian potash, cost us $65 or $70 a ton. You will readily understand therefor that the resultant yield was not nearly as good as formerly; the crop per acre in New Brunswick in 1918 was smaller than ever before. 'Consequently the cost per barrel of growing this crop of potatoes was higher. The cost per barrel is always higher when you get a small yield because the raising of potatoes is not like manufacturing an axe, a wheelbarrow or anything of that kind. It cost us that year $65 or $70 per acre for fertilizer, and it costs us so much per acre to raise potatoes regardless of whether we got a big yield 180
or a small one. We only secured a yield of fifty or sixty barrels per acre at a much greater cost per barrel than in the case of the 100 or the 125 barrels per acre which had been our usual yield in New Brunswick. In this connection I want to assure you that I know what I am talking about as I was president of the New Brunswick Potato Growers' Association for the first two years it was in operation. It was an organization formed for the better production of potatoes; it was not a commercial organization but was formed for the purpose of promoting seed selection and better methods of cultivation, and getting a larger yield per acre. No ofllcial of that organization got any salary at all; we all gave our time gratis. The New Brunswick potato growers benefited largely by that organization. The average cost per bag of raising potatoes in 1918 in New Brunswick was $1.30-that is grown and harvested. It cost the farmers about ten cents per bag to deliver them at the railway-that is the way we sell them and not in our field. The potatoes sold until some time in November for $1.50 per bag, so you will very readily see the farmers were not making large profits. When the potatoes delivered at the station cost $1.40 and we got $1.50 per bag you will see we were not making any big profit taking into consideration the work done in planting this crop. However, on the 21st of November an article appeared in several Canadian papers-and I am going to read it to you. I am not like the hon. member for Algoma East (M,r. Nicholson); I am not ashamed to give you the name of the paper and the date. I could not help thinking when the hon. member was quoting that article with regard to the way the British protected themselves by raising .prices to cut out competition that that quotation was taken from one of the Hearst publications. I was inclined to think so by the tone of it, because I think it is one of the most unusual things in the world to raise your price to cut out competition. I never was able to do it. This is the information which was sent out by the 'Canada Food Board:
Potato Crop of Canada for 1918 Set New Record. Exportable Surplus. Over and Above all Needs for Domestic Use and Seeding Canada has 28,433,000 Bushels to Send Abroad.
Ottawa, November 20.-A revised estimate of the Canadian potato crop from figures In possession of the Canada Food Board shows an exportable surplus in six provinces of 28,433,-C00 bushels over all requirements for domestic use and seeding.



It goes on to say that in the other provinces of Canada there will he none for export, but that the total export for Canada will be 28,433,000 bushels. In view of the fact that Canada had never exported more than 4,000,000 bushels in one year, you can judge what effect this had in the market in which we were selling our potatoes.-and that year we were exporting largely to the United States and Cuba. I received a letter from a prominent dealer in Cuba who had evidently got my name as President of the New Brunswick Potato Growers' Association, and perhaps he thought I was a more important man than I really was. In this letter he inquired about conditions in New Brunswick and asked if this large amount of potatoes was actually available in Canada for export. I told him that while I did not have anything but the Government report,
I did not believe any such thing, and I think that later information which I have received has fully justified that statement. However, this report had gone out. broadcast to the dealers in the United States and Cuba to whom we were shipping our potatoes, and it was natural that they should expect to get potatoes for little or nothing. Potatoes are not like wheat or hay; they are perishable, and you must sell them within a year from the time they are produced. Now, I had the export returns for that year and knew what they were, but I put a question on the Order Paper to which I received an answer on April 19th, because I wanted the Department of Agriculture to put themselves on record. I was somewhat in the position of the Minister of the Interior, who said in a recent speech in this House with regard to resolutions passed by the G.W.V.A., that he was just'a little suspicious of their motives in moving these resolutions. Well, I was just a little suspicious that my hon. friends opposite might question my figures, but I knew that they could not deny their own. The question was as follows)
What was the total export of potatoes from Canada to all countries from the crop grown in 1918, giving the number of bushels exported each month from August 1, 1918, to July 31, 1919?	[DOT]
To which the reply was:
Hon. Mr. Burrell: The total export of potatoes from Canada to all countries from August 1, 1918, to July 31, 1919, is as follows: The department has no information as to the export of potatoes as to crop grown in 1918.
The reason why I asked for the returns by the month was this: we begin to harvest our potatoes towards the end of August and we finish marketing them before the end [Mr. Caldwell.)
of the following July, because they axe perishable. Very few are shipped in July, so that shipments from August 1918 to July 1919 cover the 1918 crop. No potatoes of the former year's crop are carried over until August of the following year; nor are any left in the country from the crop of the year before to be shipped out after the end of July. Instead of 28,000,000 bushels, which the Canada Food Board stated to be the exportable surplus, these figures show a total of 4,150,847 bushels of potatoes available for export from Canada for that year.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to give you the effect of this statement which was published in the Canadian newspapers and heralded broadcast throughout the world. Up to the 24th November, about three or four days after this statement appeared in the Canadian papers, potatoes had been selling at $1.50 a hag or $3 a barrel. _ The price immediately dropped off after this: it went down to 75 cents a bag; at least half the potatoes that were exported from New Brunswick were sold at from 75 cents to $1 a bag-potatoes that cost the farmers $1.40 a hag to produce and haul to the railway siding. So you can understand that the farmers of New Brunswick were not making much money in the growing of potatoes; they were not profiteering. In March, however, the supply of potatoes ran out; this 28,000,000 bushels did not materialize and the price went up at one jump to $3 a barrel or $1.50 a bag. It advanced ' to $2.50 a hag, and there was not a sufficient supply to meet the demand. Consequently our potato growers in New Brunswick-and I think what is true of New Brunswick is true of the other potato-growing sections of Canada-in the spring of 1919 did not plant a very big acreage of potatoes, and I do not think that the people of this country can

blame them very much for that. They said: If the Government, while urging increase of acreage and of production generally and calling upon the farmers to raise a larger crop at greater expense than ever before, issue an absolutely false statement that causes us to lose 65 cents a bag on our potatoes, certainly we are not going to be caught in that trap again. As I say, therefore, the farmers planted a very short acreage of potatoes last year, and as high as $12 a barrel has been offered for them. In that connection, as I said before-and I do not fear successful contradiction-the potatoes were not in the country. Now, it may be said that this statement was sent out by some official who is no longer in the service of the Government. But I am inclined to think that the same man is there yet, because a ^further estimate was made of the quantity*of potatoes said to be in the farmers' hands' on April 24, 1920. I got the following from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics a short time ago:
Ottawa, April 24, 1920. The Dominion Bureau of Statistics issued to-day a press bulletin giving in summary form the results of its annual inquiry as to the total quantities of wheat, oats, barley and flaxseed in Canada, at the end of March, the stocks of all kinds of agricultural products remaining in farmers' 'hands at the same date.
I will give the quotation only in regard to potatoes, because it is potatoes that I am talking about. This statement says that the stock of potatoes in the farmers' hands on April 24, 1920, as stated by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics was 31,646,000 bushels, compared with 32,836,000 bushels last year and 24,130,500 bushels in 1918. Now, here is a quotation from a paper, and by the way, I am able to give the authority for this1 too; I do not believe in making any quotations without citing the authority for them. This despatch is headed: "Says Canada is Swept Clean of Potatoes." It is a Canadian press despatch dated at Montreal, April 23, the day before the statement was issued by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics to which I have referred.
Montreal, April 23,-Are American buyers invading Canada in droves to buy up every potato that can be discovered? The assertion that they are doing so is made by local dealers who give this as the greatest reason for the high price now being paid here by the housewives for the family supplies.
Here is the way a dealer sums up the situation :
"It is almost impossible to get potatoes anywhere in the provinces of Quebec, Nova Scotia New Brunswick or Prince Edward Island now." 1801
And these are the big potato-growing provinces.
"The Americans have sent swarms of buyers into the Dominion and there are four or five men bidding for everything that is available One United States buyer told us he had got five carloads at $5.75 per bag f.o.b. in Prince Edward Island ; another said he had found eighty cars for Pittsburg at the same rate. I tried to get two cars for Montreal in Prince Edward Island. After a long time I got them at $4 75 f.o.b. there for a bag of 90 lbs. It costs about 7o cents per bag to bring them on to Montreal making the cost here about $5.50. But the real reason why Montrealers are paying such enormous prices how is that the country has been swept clean of its crop by the Americans and so it has passed over the border."
I want to tell the House why the potato growers received such high prices for these potatoes. You will say: Well, the farmers are profiteering in getting such high prices for these potatoes. These were potatoes which the farmers had intended to plant his spring, and a large number of potato growers have sold half the quantity of their seed potatoes this spring, having been tempted by the high prices. Consequently, the acreage planted in potatoes will he short this year, and owing to the statement issued by the Canada Pood Board on November 21, 1918, there will be high prices for potatoes next fall because these things have far-reaching results. speechtext:
I am not going to detain the House for every long at this late hour; but I wish to discuss the Budget for a few moments and to give reasons for the course which I shall pursue when the vote takes place on the amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's. We have heard, in the discussion of the Budget, the question of protection,- moderate, adequate, and high and free trade. I have been a member of this House for about eleven years, and I -have heard that same subject discussed during all the time I have .been a member of this House. For a great part of that time I supported a Government which had as its platform ^ a policy of tariff for revenue, and I am in the same position to-night. The view which I hold is that the Government should lay down a tariff which would be productive of revenue, and I see that principle evolved in the Budget as laid down here. We have come through a series of extreme years caused by the war. We have incurred an enormous debt which has to be met, no matter what our theories or pet views may he, and I am convinced that the revenue of this country must be raised from every conceivable source. I might have the profoundest respect for the moderate tariff or tariff-for-revenue views. Under ordinary conditions a moderate tariff would supply the means for Taising the

revenue of this country, hut- under present-day conditions, with a debt of over two bilion dollars, with a sparse population such as we have, I am convinced that we have to resort to every measure of taxation to preserve the credit of Canada at this particular time.
When the question comes up, what is protection, I find this position. I have listened very carefully to this debate on the Budget this session because I took a course last year which caused me to be careful how I should go at the present time. I have listened very carefully to the arguments brought forward as to how the revenue might be raised. I have listened to hon. gentlemen of the progressive party telling us how they would raise the revenue, but I have failed up to this moment to hear one constructive speech, which would lead me to believe that they could raise the necessary money to carry on the affairs of this country by any programme they have brought forward. The amendment of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has left me in the same quandry. If -that amendment were carried, logically it defeats all the proposals under the present Budget. It does away with the income tax, it does away with the luxury tax, it does away with the sales tax. It obliterates all the new proposals and says:	We want to assist
the consumer by reducing tariff taxation. Now that does not commend itself to my best thought. I do not believe it is logical. I do not believe the people of this country would take me seriously if I would support an amendment of that kind under presentrday conditions.
I do not for one moment want any one to imagine that I have discarded any of the beliefs which I hold as to what constitutes a tariff in this country. We hear the question of adequate or moderate protection raised. I have made many inquiries as to what protection means. To my mind any tariff, whether it is five per cent or ten per cent, constitutes protection to a certain degree. I cannot conceive of any tariff being placed on goods imported into this country which would not afford some measure of protection. To that extent I am a protectionist.
When we consider the plan for raising the revenue put forward on behalf of opponents of the Government we are confronted with the platform put forward by the official Opposition. To my mind, it is a good platform. If the official Opposition would go further, and if I believed that
the people of this country thought that they would raise the revenue under the platform which has been laid down, I should find no fault with it. But I am convinced, as I stated before, that that platform is not sufficient to raise the necessary revenue for this country under present conditions.
I commend the Government for the imposition of an income tax. It is a true Liberal principle. It is a direct tax. I commend them also for the new Budget proposals. I perhaps might criticise the details of the presumed luxury tax. I think $9 for a pair of shoes may not be the proper basis for exemption. I do not think $45 for a suit of clothes is the proper basis for exemption. I am positive that $5 for a hat is not the proper basis for exemption. I am also sure that $5 for underwear is not the proper basis for exemption. But these are matters of detail. The principle is there that those who can pay must pay, and if the effect is to curb extravagance then I am heart and! soul in favour of the tax. When it comes to the question of the sales tax, we hear the statement made on all bands, why, the consumer pays it. Certainly he pays it. We are all consumers in this country, and how can we avoid paying it? It makes no difference how the taxes are imposed, the consumer pays them, because there is nobody else to pay them.
As to this question of the manufacturer absorbing, the manufacturer absorbs just ias much as his business will permit him to absorb, just as my hon. friend from Garleton (Mr. Caldwell) absorbs the potato crop. Just so far as he can get the price, just that fax is the absorption. That is taken up by all manufacturers, wholesalers, retailers and other distributers. I have no brief for any of the merchandising class, but my judgment is that in this Dominion *of Canada our trade is conducted along as honourable lines as in any other country. I am of opinion that the less restrictions we put on trade the better it is for the country, and when we get rid of this tremendous load we are carrying at the present time, I say, give us all the freedom of trade that we can have. In the meantime we are dealing with conditions which must be met, and in my judgment the present proposals put forward by the Minister of Finance are the best proposals that I have heard from any party in this House, and I therefore intend to support the Budget.
